edits.chapter_key: the author and his only book
edits.body_md:
The book's name is *Kunooz al-Hikmah al-madhkurah li-arbab al-ismah* — The Stored Treasures of Wisdom for the Masters of Infallibility. These are treasures of wisdom preserved for the *arbab al-ismah* (أَرْبَابُ الْعِصْمَةِ), the masters of infallibility. The *arbab al-ismah* are those who possess *'ismah* (عِصْمَة), infallibility. In one sense the phrase points to the Ahl al-Bayt (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) and their progeny, but that is not the meaning intended here. The Ahl al-Bayt and the *Aimmah Tahirin* (أَئِمَّة طَاهِرِين), the Pure Imams, are the masters of *kulli ismah* (كُلِّيِّ عِصْمَة), total infallibility — it is impossible for them to err, and they are free from all sin. The *duat* (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ), by contrast, are the masters of *juzi ismah* (جُزْئِي عِصْمَة), partial infallibility. This distinction was clarified in a *risalah* (رِسَالَةٌ) by Sayyidna Ali ibn Hussain al-Jamari, who explained that the *Aimmah Tahirin* are the masters of *kulli ismah*, while the *duat*, and especially the *qaimi duat* (قَائِمِي دُعَاةٍ), the standing *duat*, are the masters of *juzi ismah*. These matters have been stored for the *duat* — the *arbab al-ismah* of *juzi ismah* — so that they may draw new understanding from them.

The book was written by Sayyidna Ali ibn Hibatullah, known as al-Shamsi, a figure of great station. Sayyidna Hibatullah Sahib — that is, Sayyidna Hibatullah ibn Ibrahim — had several children, and he performed *nass* (نَصٌّ), designation, upon his eldest son. That eldest child was Sayyidna Ali ibn 'Ibad, whose full lineage runs: Sayyidna Ali ibn Hibatullah ibn Ibrahim ibn Muhammad, the *shajarah*, or family tree, continuing without interruption all the way back to Adam (عَلَيْهِ السَّلَامُ). Sayyidna Ali ibn Ibad, however, passed away during his father's lifetime, and so he became a *ghayr-munfarid Dai* (غَيْرُ مُنْفَرِد دَاعٍ), a non-independent *Dai* (دَاعِي). Sayyidna Hibatullah Sahib then performed *nass* upon another son, who became eighth in the order of succession — the rank Sayyidna Ali ibn Ibad had held at his death. Sayyidna Ali ibn Ibad had himself performed *nass* upon yet another son, Sayyidna Ismail (إِسْمَاعِيل), who was tenth in the order of succession. It is said that Sayyidna Ismail ibn Hibatullah possessed the most excellent outward form — *surat* (صُورَة) — in the community, *jamaat* (جَمَاعَة), of the *wulat* (وُلَاة). Another child of Sayyidna Hibatullah Sahib was Sayyidna Hasan ibn Ibad, who likewise became a *Dai* of great station. Yet another was Sayyidna Jafar (جَعْفَر), who was the seventy-fourth *Dai*. He did not reach the rank of *Dai* in succession, yet his station is great, and he composed *qasaid*, odes, among other works.

The book *al-Kawakib al-Durriyah*, itself a work of great station, opens with a *qasidah* (قَصِيدَة) by Sayyidna Jafar ibn Hibatullah.

As for Sayyidna Ali ibn Hibatullah, he wrote only one *risalah* — only this single book, nothing besides. He wrote it during his father's lifetime. His station among the *duat* is nonetheless exceedingly high.

*Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim*. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Above the *Bismillah* is written the *Ism al-Azam* (الِاسْمُ الْأَعْظَم), the Greatest Name. In the *risalah* by Sayyidna al-Wajih — that is, 'Abd al-Ali (عَلِي) ibn Hasan al-Wajih — great wonders and secrets are set down, and the entire *risalah* addresses a single question: whether the *Ism al-Azam* is greater, or whether the *nur*, the light, of the *Bismillah* is greater. After a lengthy discussion, he concluded that the *nur* of the *Ism al-Azam* is more excellent than that of *Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim*. That is why the *Ism al-Azam* is written above the *Bismillah*.

The script in which it appears is *khatt al-Teseri*, the Teseri script. In this script the first dot is a *khatam* (خَاتَمٌ) — a seal, that is, a ring — and this ring alludes to the *Ahl al-Sharif* (أَهْلُ الشَّرَف), the noble family. The three marks above it carry their own significance. There are also verses, *ashar*, by Amir al-Muminin on the *Ism al-Azam*. The *madd* (مَدٌّ) — the elongation mark above it — refers to the *muawanah*, the assistance, received from the *Hudud 'Aliyah* (حُدُودٌ عَالِيَة), the higher ranks of the hierarchy; the *madd* points toward that. The precise details are not at hand at present, but God willing, should the occasion arise, they will be brought forward. That is a matter separate from the present text.

The book at hand is *Kunooz al-Hikmah al-madhkura li-arbab al-ismah*, The Treasures of Wisdom Mentioned for the People of *'Ismah*. That is the name of the book, and it is the work of Sayyidna Ali ibn Hibatullah al-Mukarrami.

*Audhu billahi minash shaytanir rajim.* (I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan.) *Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim.* (In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.) *Wa bihi nastain, sallallahu 'ala rasulihi Sayyidina Muhammadin wa ala aali Sayyidina Muhammadin wa barik wa sallim.* (And in Him we seek help. May God's blessings, peace, and benedictions be upon His messenger, our master Muhammad, and upon the family of our master Muhammad.)

Sayyidna Ali ibn Ibad, however, passed away during his father's lifetime, and so he became a *ghayr-munfarid Dai*, a non-independent *Dai*. *Wal-hamdulillahi rabbil-alamin.* (And all praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds.)

<!-- editorial:begin -->
> **Editorial note (tradition-grounded).** 
> *A note on terms.* When this chapter speaks of the *Hudud 'Aliyah*, the higher ranks, the word
> repays a look at its root. *Hudud* is the plural of *hadd*, the boundary or limit that marks
> where one thing ends and another begins; the root h-d-d means to set an edge — whether a
> physical border or a sharpened blade — and from it also comes *hadid*, iron, the hard and
> cutting metal. In the wider usage of this tradition the same word names the fixed limits God has
> set, and by extension the defined penalties for crossing them. Read this way, the ranks of the
> hierarchy are not merely levels but thresholds: each is a defined edge, and the assistance the
> chapter says flows down from the higher ranks passes across precisely such ordered boundaries.
<!-- editorial:end -->

edits.chapter_key: blessings on the chain: imams, gates, and the duat of najran
edits.body_md:
*Wa 'alal aimmati min dhurriyyatihi majami' al-anwar* — and upon the Imams from his progeny, the assemblages of lights. The phrase *majami al-anwar* (مَجَامِعُ الْأَنْوَارِ) carries a precise sense. *Anwar* (أَنْوَارٌ) (lights) and *asrar* (أَسْرَار) (secrets) are two different things. *Asrar* is used for *niyyat* (intention). Concerning *anwar*: Sayyidna Sulayman has written in this very book that he is the *jami al-asrar* — the assembler of secrets — of the *duat* of Yemen who became *duat* after Sayyidna Dhuayb bin Musa. There the word used is *asrar*, not *anwar*. And *anwar* refers to the *suwarat* (صُورات), the luminous forms, of which he is the assembler.

*Wa asma al-ayn al-azimah fil-ali min al-asrar* — and the names of the great essence in the high secrets. These *Aimmah Tahirin* are the names of the great essence, dwelling in the great and high secrets. The great essence, and all the *Aimmah* who come until the Day of Resurrection, are veiled by him; he is their *hijab* (veil). These Imams are a *hijab*, and their veiled one is Amir al-Muminin.

*Wa 'ala Imam al-zaman al-mutawari bil-hijabi* — and upon the Imam of the Time, who is concealed by the veil. *Al-mustatir bil-sirr an jami' al-baraa* — the one who is hidden by the secret from all of creation. The original self remains hidden, and what has appeared is a *hijab*.

*Wa sallama 'alayhim wa ala abwabihim al-mutalali' anwaruhum fis-suwar* — and may (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) and upon their *abwab* (gates), whose lights shine forth in the forms.

*Wa 'ala hujajihim wa ala duat hadha al-dawr al-maymun al-qain khamsina alfa sanah mimma tauddun* — and upon their *hujjahs*, and upon the *duat* of this auspicious *dawr* (دَوْرٌ) (era), which will last for fifty thousand years of what you count.

The blessing falls upon the *duat* of this *dawr* — the *dawr* of the Qaim, may God's (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ). This *dawr* will last for fifty thousand years. The number has its source in this: when the Qaim comes, fifty thousand years begin after him. The present era is therefore included within it. The *dawr al-satr* (دَوْرُ السَّتْر) (era of concealment) ended with Sayyidna Sulayman Sahib; the seven eras were finished — as confirmed by calculation as well — and this *dawr* is included in the *dawr* of the Qaim. Hence the words *al-qain khamsina alfa sanah mimma tauddun*.

*Wa Sulayman bin Hasan al-mujtama ladayhi asraru duat al-Yaman* — and Sulayman bin Hasan, with whom are gathered the secrets of the *duat* of Yemen. The secrets were gathered in his keeping alone — a station of great distinction.

*Wa Jafar al-sabi fis-sirr al-mamun* — and Jafar, the seventh in the protected secret. Jafar is the seventh: being the twenty-eighth, he became the seventh in the manifest, protected secret.

*Wa mimun min lala* — and a Mim (مِيم) from above. Mim refers to Muhammad bin Fuad (مُحَمَّد بِن فُؤَاد), that intermediate figure who came in between, non-independent though he was.

*Al-qaim bi-fard al-jihad fi malain* — the one who established the duty of jihad among the assembly. He is the one who establishes the duty of jihad in the midst of the assembly — that is, among the people. His jihad was tremendous. Had the position of Sayyidna Muhammad bin Fuad been ruined — as happened in the case of Abd al-Muttalib and others — the *dawah* itself would have stood in peril, and its history would have changed entirely. Yet the jihad he carried out was tremendous.

*Wa al-ayn al-mutafajjir 'ala lisanihi yanabi' al-asrar* — and 'Ayn (عَيْن), upon whose tongue gushed forth the springs of secrets. Ayn means Sayyidna Ali bin Sulayman (سَيِّدُنَا عَلِيُّ بْنُ سُلَيْمَانَ), from whose tongue the springs of secrets gushed forth. The various secrets of the doctrines — their springs and fountains — were made manifest through his tongue. In his *haqaiq* (حَقَائِق) and his other books he presented sublime matters of doctrine, things that had not been presented before. Of *Shual al-Anwar*, which is the first book, he himself wrote that this *Shual al-Anwar* is in the *haqaiq* (realities) and the *daqaiq* (دَقَائِق) (subtleties): *hadha al-kitab fil haqaiq wad-daqaiq*. From there the books of subtleties began.

Sayyidna Jafar did not write a single book on *haqaiq*. All his books are on *hujjat* (حُجَّة) (proof) or *tawil* (تَأْوِيل) (interpretation), although his own station is very lofty. Mim and 'Ayn are often mentioned to refer to the *muhtajib* (مُحْتَجِب), but here they are used to refer to the *duat*.

*Al-ati bi-ma la yakhtur 'alal afkar* — bringing forth that which had never occurred to the thoughts. He brought forth things that had never crossed people's minds and had never before been made manifest. The books that stand in his name — *Anwar al-Shashaniyyah* and others — and the lofty realities within them, are very special things that he presented.

*Wa saribuhu alladhi ghada ghidha al-nufus bi-asrar al-malakut al-quddus* — and his drinking companion, who became the nourishment of souls with the secrets of the holy *malakut* (مَلَكُوت). His *sarib*, his drinking companion, means Sayyidna Ibrahim. He became the nourishment of souls with the secrets of the holy *malakut* — from the secrets of Allah, the Holy.

*Wa Muhammaduhu al-muhajir min baldatihi li-uluwwi shanih wa rutbatihi* — and his Muhammad, the emigrant from his town for the loftiness of his station and his rank. Muhammad here means Muhammad bin Ismail (مُحَمَّد بِن إِسْمَاعِيل). He is the first *Dai* who emigrated from his town, to Najran. Until then the *dawah* had been in Yemen: in Sanaa, in Haraz, and in Safan. He is the first *Dai* who left Yemen and came to Najran, for the loftiness of his station and rank. He is also the first and only *Dai* who was given permission to lead prayers in *ghayr jazirah* (غَيْرِ جَزِيرَة) — outside the Arabian peninsula — and so he led prayers in Habasha.

After him, the *duat* did not simply return to Yemen. A few remained where they were, and then they too moved. It was in the time of Sayyidna Hasan Shihab and Sayyidna Ali bin 'Ibad that they were there, and in the time of Sayyidna Ghulam Hussain Sahib they came fully to Najran — though in fact this was somewhat earlier.

The emigration was toward Najran, and there was also the going to Abuna, to Sayyidna Muhammad bin Ismail. Sayyidna Sulayman Sahib, in his time, toured Abuna and stayed there for quite some time. The journey from Yemen to India was one of great hardship, taking one year and passing through various cities of Syria and elsewhere. There was a stay in Abuna as well, and a mosque was built there which still exists today. Sayyidna Hussain bin Hasan later enlarged that mosque, and in the time of Sayyidna Hussain bin Ismail it was further expanded and rooms were built for those sitting in *itikaf* (اعْتِكَاف) (seclusion). It is a very magnificent mosque.

Abuna is not a port. It is a mountainous area, very far from the coast — about two hundred kilometers from Najran, remote and mountainous. Sayyidna Sahib went there, and it has been visited in later times as well. The grave of Sayyidna Rashid, Rashid bin 'Isa, is also there, and the grave was visited and the *ziyarat* (زِيَارَة) performed. Sayyidna Rashid is the one who, after becoming a *Dai*, stood for six years in his prayer niche making up his missed prayers. It is possible that in the early period of the *dawah* some prayers were missed, and he made up six years of them standing in the prayer niche.

After the passing of Sayyidna Hussain bin Hasan, Sayyidna Hussain bin Ismail gave one of their companions — Ahmad by name, a boy from Yemen, very intelligent and an exceptionally good young man — the prayers of Sayyidna Hussain bin Hasan: four years of prayers that had been missed, for in those last days he had become like an angel and could not keep track of his prayers. So four years of prayers were made up. And when Sayyidna Hussain bin Hasan passed away, the walk to his side was made barefoot from the house — a considerable distance, of the order of the distance from there to Grand Road station — and it was covered barefoot.

*Sallam 'alayhim ajmain abad al-abadin* — forever and ever. May peace be upon all of them, for all time.

*Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim.*

*Fatiha.*

*Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim...*

*Fatiha.*

*Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim...*

> **Editorial note (tradition-grounded).** 
> *An editorial aside:* Readers meeting the language of gathered *asrar* and the *haqaiq* of
> *Shual al-Anwar* for the first time may find help in a related teaching preserved in this
> tradition, which speaks of the tree in Eden in its good sense as pointing to "the knowledge of
> realities, which is forbidden to those who are not worthy of it" — a knowledge belonging to the
> Imams, whose attainment "gives rise to eternity and brings release from this perishing bodily
> world." That framing explains why such secrets are described as gathered in a single trusted
> keeper rather than broadcast: restriction here is a matter of worthiness, not of withholding.
> The same wider tradition connects the theme of concealment to the very beginning of the human
> cycle, describing Adam, peace be upon him, as the one who began the cycle of concealment — a
> useful backdrop to the vocabulary of veil and hidden secret used throughout this chapter.
<!-- editorial:end -->

*Nasut* and *lahut* stand in relation to the negation and the affirmation within the word of the *shahadah*, just as negation and affirmation belong to Allah Taala, the possessor of might and power — `li 'izzat wal-jabarut` (for the Almighty and the All-Powerful).

`Wa lil-imam 'alayhi al-salam thalathat hujub` (And for the Imam, (ع), there are three veils). The Imam has three veils — three at the foundation, though other veils are also employed. `Mathalu thalathat jawahir (جَوَاهِرُ) al-nizam` (The example of the three jewels of the order). Just as the word of the *shahadah* contains three jewels — *alif* (أَلِفٌ), *lam*, *ha* — so likewise the Imam has three veils. These point toward three forms of *nasut*:

- *nasut-e-tabii* (the natural human form)
- *nasut-e-zilli* (the shadowy human form)
- *nasut-e-khas* (the special human form)

`Wa kullu imam min mawlana husayn jamaa rutub al-arbaah` (And every Imam from our master Husayn has combined the four ranks). Every Imam from Imam Husayn onward has combined all four ranks.

What occurred with Imam Hasan and Imam Husayn requires explanation. Imam Hasan held two ranks, and Imam Husayn held two ranks. In Imam Hasan's time, the two higher ranks — the ranks of Imamate and succession — belonged to Imam Hasan, which is why he was the Imam: whoever holds the higher ranks is the Imam of the time. The two lower ranks were with Imam Husayn, by virtue of which he stood under the authority of Imam Hasan.

This same pattern had governed earlier ages. Among the progeny of Sayyidna Ibrahim, whoever held the two higher ranks was the Imam of that time. Qaydar was there; Mawlana Ismail was there; and the other Imams of those ages — all of them held the two higher ranks. The prophets of their time held the two lower ranks and were entrusted with the mission. Within the progeny of Sayyidna Ibrahim, and specifically within the progeny of Mawlana Ismail, the same arrangement held: Sayyidna Ismail held the two higher ranks, while the prophet of that time, Ishaq, held the two lower ranks. That pattern continued throughout history.

After the passing of Imam Hasan, all four ranks came together with Imam Husayn and were never divided again. All subsequent Imams held all four. Yet the first Imam with whom the four ranks were truly and fully united was Mawlana Ali Zayn al-Abidin. Even with Imam Husayn, the two lower ranks had dominated over the higher ones, and he too had been subject to that dominance. Once the four ranks were united in Mawlana Ali Zayn al-Abidin, his station was elevated above all preceding Imams. That is why he is called the *Adam-e-Aal-e-Aba* — the Adam of the Prophet's family. Just as Adam was the first of his kind, Mawlana Ali Zayn al-Abidin became the Adam of the Ahl al-Bayt (the People of the House).

A question was raised: did the Messenger also hold the four ranks, and were those ranks given as a trust to Mawlana Ali?

The Messenger did hold the four ranks. With Sayyidna Rasulullah, the two higher ranks were likewise gathered with him — but held as a trust (أَمَانَة). After Mawlana Abd al-Muttalib, the four ranks that had been with him were distributed: he gave the two higher ranks to Mawlana Abu Talib, since Sayyidna Abdullah had already passed away. A grandfather may bequeath to a grandson, so those two remaining ranks were kept as a trust with Sayyidna Abu Talib, on behalf of Sayyidna Rasulullah. When the time came for the appointment of Sayyidna Ali as Imam, Sayyidna Abu Talib gave all four ranks to Sayyidna Rasulullah. The two ranks of mission and prophethood had been descending from Sayyidna Abd al-Muttalib and were rightfully Sayyidna Rasul's. The two ranks of Imamate, however, were given to Sayyidna Rasulullah as a trust — meant for Ali. For Ali. And so:

> `man kuntu mawlahu fa hadha 'aliyyun mawlahu`

Of whomsoever I am the master, Ali is his master. Of whomsoever he was the master — meaning the master of these ranks — Ali is his master. That is the meaning.

`Wa mathalu arbaat rutub... al-muqattaat al-arbaah fil-kalimat al-shahadah: La, ilaha, illa, Allah` (And the example of the four ranks is the four sections in the word of the *shahadah*: La, ilaha, illa, Allah).

`Wa istirahat al-maqam fis-sabi min al-ayimmah` (And the resting of the station is in the seventh of the Imams). The seventh Imam is called the station of rest. With him, the accomplishments of the six preceding Imams are gathered, making it a restful station — one where nothing further remains to be added. The seventh becomes the *jami*, the gatherer. `Min al-ayimmah al-qaim... li man sabaqahu min al-ruh` (From the Imams, the *qaim* — one who rises — for those who preceded him of the spirit). For the past Imams, he becomes a station of the spirit. `Mathalu sabat fusul (فُصُول) fil-shahadah` (The example of the seven sections in the *shahadah*). There are seven sections in the word of the *shahadah*: when it is written in the Arabic manner, there are seven places where the pen lifts from the surface of the paper. Those seven liftings of the pen point to the station of the seventh — the *sabi* (سَابِع) — who is the *jami*, and whose rank is very high.

`Wal-imam majma suwar ithna 'ashar jazirah bil-akhir` (And the Imam is the confluence of the forms of the twelve islands in the end). `Mathalu ithna ashar harfan fil-shahadah al-kabirah` (The example of the twelve letters in the great *shahadah*). The Imam is the confluence: the forms of the twelve islands — the twelve *duat* (summoners) — converge with the Imam at the end, just as there are twelve letters in the word of the great *shahadah*.

`Wa jamee dhalika... thamaniah wa 'ishruna... suratan haddan... nizam al-alam al-ala (نِظَامُ الْعَالَمِ الْأَعْلَى) sarmada` (And the total of all of that is twenty-eight forms as a limit… the order of the higher world, eternally). Added together, two and three and four and seven and twelve become twenty-eight, which is the *nizam al-alam al-ala* — the order of the higher world — eternal. That is a discussion unto itself.

A question was raised concerning the *falak-e-muheet*, which ascends without coming to earth: whether it goes and meets the *barzakh-e-ashir*. The answer given was that this has not been mentioned, or has not been read. It was then observed that there is a verse of the Quran:

> `yanfudhuna la tanfudhuna illa bi sultan`

They pass through; they cannot pass through except with an authority.

Whatever is ascending therefore waits in the *barzakh-e-ashir* until the authority comes. It is deduced from that verse that the same applies to the *falak-e-ashir*. It is not stated explicitly in the text, but the deduction leads there.

Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. This reading of the Fatiha is made a gift — a means of connection, lofty, pure, and pleasing — to the soul of Sayyidna Ali ibn Hibatullah, may Allah sanctify his soul, may his grace be upon us, and may Allah increase us in his blessings. O Allah, accept from us this benefit and the benefiting from it, for the sake of what is contained within it, for the sake of Sayyidna Muhammad and his progeny (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ). Al-Fatiha. And for the sake of Sayyidna al-Dai al-Mutlaq, the chief of the two *dawahs* (الدَّعْوَتَيْن), the *zill* (ظِلّ) (shadow) of the *hadd* (حَدّ) of Sindh, the honor of the noble, the pride of the Arabs and non-Arabs, our master Sayyidna Muhammad Burhanuddin, may Allah sanctify his soul and his sacred mausoleum, may Allah elevate his station and prolong his life, and grant the visit to his noble presence, and for the sake of Sayyidna al-Dai al-Mutlaq, Mawlana Mufaddal Saifuddin, may Allah prolong his noble life. Al-Fatiha.

> **Editorial note (tradition-grounded).** 
> *A note for the reader.* The tradition preserves a saying about the two brothers whose shared
> ranks this chapter describes: "Hasan and Husayn are two Imams of truth, whether they rise or
> sit, and their father is better than them both" — a formulation that affirms the Imamate of each
> while still ordering them beneath Ali, much as the discussion above distinguishes higher ranks
> from lower without denying either brother his standing. On the "twelve islands," a modern reader
> may find the word puzzling: *jazirah* here is not geography but a region of the summons, and the
> wider tradition uses the term in just this way when it speaks of those who were "sent into the
> islands" and received commands there rather than in the presences directly. The islands are thus
> the outward field of the call, gathered back at the end to the Imam who is their confluence.

edits.chapter_key: the black stone and the cycles of return
edits.body_md:
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. In Him is all help sought, and may Allah's blessings and peace be upon His Messenger, our Master Muhammad, and the family of Muhammad.

These two are the counterparts of the Kalima-e-Shahadat already mentioned. Sayyidna Ali bin Hibatullah (سَيِّدُنَا عَلِيّ بِن هِبَةِ اللَّه) said:

"fa-sun hadha al-sirr al-masun, yasunaka Allah, wa-hfaz ma ulqiya ilayka, yahfazaka Allah, wa hadha min al-asrar al-izam allati la yakad yastur bil-aqlam, wa dhalika mimma ajrahu."

"Guard this preserved secret, and Allah will guard you. Preserve what has been cast upon you, and Allah will preserve you. This is among the great secrets that pens can scarcely set down, and it is from what He has caused to flow."

These are matters of the most magnificent secrets — of a nature that cannot be committed to writing. Whatever has been written here flowed upon the tongue by the grace of the Mawla. Sayyidna Hibatullah said of them:

"wa lam yakun qabla dhalika tara fi qalbi wa janani, wa hiya nuqtah min bahri 'ulumihi wa hibatihi, wa tuhfatun min tuhafihi, wa sadaqa min sadaqatihi, wa qad saqatha ayyuha al-... ilayka hadiyah mubaradah bi-ghayri taabin alayka, wa mathaluha la yahsul illa bil-ibtila wal-hijr wal-hijrat wal-firaq lil-ahl wal-awtan, fa-ahmad mawlaka fi ghuduwwika wa masaka."

"Before this, these matters had not arisen in my heart or my soul. It is a single drop from the ocean of his knowledges and his gifts, a gift from among his gifts, a charity from his charities. These things have reached you, O brother, as a cooling gift that brings peace, without any toil on your part. Their like is not attained except through trial, through separation and emigrations, through leaving one's family, one's cities, and one's homelands. So praise your Master in your morning and in your evening."

No effort was made, and yet this came. Seated in one place, what others obtain only through exile was obtained.

Then the third question: "qad 'alimtu mimma jawwaba Zain al-Abidin ala Umm al-Nada (أُمُّ النَّدَى) min qabli... umr al-dunya" — "I have already taken note of what Mawlana Zain al-Abidin answered to Umm al-Nada concerning the age of the world." Umm al-Nada was a woman of great standing, among the Hudud al-Dawat and a woman of deep learning. She came to Imam Zain al-Abidin (ع) and said, "Mawlana, tell me how much time has passed over the world, and how much remains." He replied, "I will tell you how much has passed, but I will not tell you how much remains. You do not have the istihqaq (merit) for that." He then told her that one mawr had passed, and that they were living within the kawr — the dawr — of the second mawr.

The questioner continued: "wa qad qala Sayyidna al-Qadi Sarim al-Din qaddas Allahu nafsahu wa razaqna shafaatahu bi-ridaka 'anna, anna al-rukn min fudulat (فُضُولَات) Amir al-Muminin al-qadimah fi al-akwar al-ula" — that Sayyidna al-Qadi Sarim al-Din, may Allah sanctify his soul and grant the provision of his intercession and be pleased with them, has said that the Rukn is from the ancient remnants of the Commander of the Faithful in the first cycles.

Sarim al-Din is Sayyidna Ibrahim bin Muhammad Faad, the questioner's grandfather. The Rukn al-Asad — spelled alif, sin, ayn, dal — is the most blessed corner of the Baytullah, the corner in which the Hajar al-Aswad is set. This Rukn al-Asad, it is said, is composed of the fudulat (remnants) of Amir al-Muminin from the first akwar (cycles). This was set down "fi waraqatayni bi-khatti Sayyidi Safi al-Din Ahmad bin Ismail" — "in two pages in the hand of Safi al-Din Ahmad bin Ismail," who was among the Hudud of that era — "fi awwal al-jussah al-mudhamam," in the first great corporeal form. In those first akwar, Amir al-Muminin underwent the rajat (return) repeatedly, born and then passing away, and through successive cycles their accumulated fudulat formed the Rukn al-Asad.

From this arose further questions: "wa fi ayyi kawr zahara amruhu, wa kayfa kana zuhuruhu, wa hal yaqiu 'alayhi al-subhaniyyah... wa kam min hadha umr al-dunya" — "In which cycle did his affair appear, and in what manner did it manifest? And does the term Subhaniyyah apply to him? And how much of the age of the world has this encompassed?" The specific question about Subhaniyyah is this: when one says "Subhan Allah," is it permissible to apply the word "Subhan" to Amir al-Muminin as well?

A questioner raised a difficulty concerning the fudulat of Amir al-Muminin: the Aimmah are all riyat, and from the perspective of the purity of their din, fudulat are not generated in their case at all.

The answer given was that the question is a good one. What fudulat means here is not what fudulah means in the case of an ordinary Mumin. In the case of the Aimmah, all such matter becomes riyat and departs; within three days, what remains is confined to the grave, and the rest becomes flowing riyat. What fudulat means here is their remaining parts. As was explained in a previous lesson, their riyat, which are stored, are housed in the Baytullah and divided into five portions. One portion goes to the Hudud al-Dawat, through which they arrive at correct decisions, are preserved from evils, and their standard in taqwa (تَقْوَى) (piety) is elevated. That one-fifth portion of their riyat is also called fudulat in one sense, and it is returned to the Baytullah when the Imam passes away. So fudulat here means their riyat in a progressed state, and those progressed riyat come to the Baytullah.

The questioner objected that this has taken a material form — that the Rukn al-Asad has been formed, that a stone has been formed. The answer was that it is not material in that sense. The nature of the Rukn al-Asad itself is lofty; what is being pointed to are the blessings within the stone.

The questioner then said that the teaching regarding the blessed stones — 'aqiq (عَقِيق) and yaqut (ruby), which are the fudulat of the Duat Kiram — is readily understandable, but that the fudulat of Mawla Ali and the Aimmah Kiram are all riyat. The answer was that fudulat in the ordinary sense are not generated in their case. In one sense alone are they called fudulat: the remaining matter left from their bodies. Sometimes riyat are also called fudulat. Those fudulat progress through the moon and ascend to Jupiter; one part of them descends and forms the body of the coming Imam, and some part comes to the Baytullah, where one-fifth is received by the Hudud al-Dawat. It also occurs that the fudulat of Amir al-Muminin — which have progressed and exist in a purified state — come to the Rukn al-Asad of the Baytullah. The word fudulat in this passage raised the same question when it was first read; what is meant by it here is riyat.

The question closed:

"wa qad tabaddala al-mashriq maghriban wal-shimal junuban. tafaddalu bil-jawab al-shafi. tawwala Allahu subhanahu bi-amarikum."

"And the east has become the west, and the north has become the south. Do us the favor of the sufficient answer. May Allah, glory be to Him, lengthen your lives."

The answer: "al-jawab 'ala dhalika al-sual, naqulu bi-awn Allah al-Kabir al-Mutaal wa minnat Wali al-Asr wal-Zaman (وَلِيُّ الْعَصْرِ وَالزَّمَانِ), alayhi salawat al-Rahim al-Rahman" — "The answer to that question: we say, with the help of Allah, the Great, the Most High, and with the grace of the Master of the Age and the Time, upon whom be the blessings of the Merciful, the Compassionate" — and with the support of Mawla al-Alam and his brilliant and magnificent secret, meaning the support of Hibatullah Sahab. "awrada Sayyidna Sarim al-Din... bi-anna al-Hajar al-Aswad min kathif Amir al-Muminin al-muwajjad" — "Sayyidna Sarim al-Din has presented the matter thus: that the Hajar al-Aswad is from the kathif of Amir al-Muminin al-muwajjad," may Allah sanctify him in Illiyyin.

By kathif (كَثِيف) is meant those riyat which are purified and which find a place in various noble stations. One such noble station is that they become the very body of the Imam — the body of the Imam who is to come. Throughout his life, the food consumed by the present Imam, and the food consumed by the future child, is all riyat. And because the Muminin are connected to those Imams and profess their walayat (allegiance), they receive a share of that sustenance.

So it is in Surah al-Furqan, in the verses concerning 'ibad al-Rahman (servants of the Merciful):

"wa-jalna lil-muttaqin imama"

"And make us an Imam for the righteous."

A man was once circumambulating the Baytullah reciting this verse, for it appears among the verses of tawaf (طَوَاف). Imam Jafar al-Sadiq, or Mawlana Ali Zain al-Abidin, said to that man: "You have asked Allah for something far beyond your station. You cannot become the Imam of the righteous; you do not have that standing." Though it is a Quranic verse, in dua (supplication) one should instead say "wa-jalna min al-muttaqin," meaning: make us from among the righteous.

"fa-dhalika huwa al-haqq alladhi la shakka yatarihi wal-sirr al-khafi alladhi la maryata fihi."

"That is the truth which no doubt can befall, and the hidden secret in which there is no ambiguity."

Then: "wa amma qawluka, wa fi ayyi kawr zahara sallallahu 'alayhi wa alihi al-ghur" — "As for your question about in which kawr he appeared, blessings upon him and his luminous family" — "faqad qala al-Nabi alayhi al-salam, ana ibn al-karrat (أَنَا ابْنُ الْكَرَّاتِ) wa mumtahin al-awqat," the Prophet ﷺ said:

"ana ibn al-karrat wa mumtahin al-awqat."

"I am the son of the recurring cycles and the one tried by the times."

Birth has come across various recurring cycles, and testing across various ages. In one narration he said: "Allah tested me seven times before the risalat (prophethood), and seven times after." Amir al-Muminin likewise says: "Rasulullah tested me seven times before making me his wasi (successor), and seven times after." He recited the full list of all fourteen tests in a single gathering, asking, "Did this not happen?" — and the entire gathering testified: "Yes, you speak the truth; it happened just so." The Awliya Allah (friends of Allah) all pass through such tests.

Testing is intrinsic to the system of the dawat (دَعْوَة) (mission). Until a person is made to pass through a test, he is not established in a rank. Sayyidna Yusuf bin Sulayman, the first Dai in Hindustan and the grandfather of Sayyidna Sulayman Sahab, was a man of great standing and magnificence. The last Dai of the Bani Anf was Sayyidna Dai Muhammad Husayn, after whom no further duat came from that line, and he put Yusuf bin Sulayman through a most severe test.

Yusuf bin Sulayman lived in a distant village and would come early each morning to study with Sayyidna Sahab. One day he arrived and the hajib (حَاجِب) — the guard of Sayyidna Muhammad bin Husayn — told him to go back, saying the Sayyidna did not wish to receive him. For forty days he came continuously at his usual hour, and each time he was turned away. On the fortieth day the hajib said, "Go away." But at that very moment the Dai called out from his veranda: "Let Yusuf come to me." He came, and the Dai embraced him. That was the test. In this way, through various such trials, he was made ready.

Sayyidna Husayn bin Ismail (سَيِّدُنَا حُسَيْنُ بْنُ إِسْمَاعِيلَ) once remarked that there were two periods in the dawat when the Hindustani muhajirin (emigrants) outnumbered the muhajirin of Yemen and Najran: the time of Sayyidna Yusuf bin Sulayman, and the time of Sayyidna Hibatullah Sahab.

"wa qad suila Mawlana al-Sadiq haythu qala, kunna fil-adwar al-madiyyah wal-huqub al-khaliyah."

"Mawlana al-Sadiq was asked, and he said: We were in the past cycles and the bygone eras."

In the cycles that have passed, there was presence. Of Aristotle he said:

"Kana Aba Muhammad Aristatalis minna Ahl al-Bayt."

"Aba Muhammad Aristotle was from us, the People of the House."

Imam Jafar al-Sadiq even mentioned his kunyah (patronymic): Aristatalis, whose title was Aba Muhammad, was from the Ahl al-Bayt. Of Salman al-Farsi he likewise said:

"Salman minna Ahl al-Bayt, yusalla wa yusallam 'alayhi."

"Salman is from us, the People of the House; blessings and peace are to be sent upon him."

The blessings sent upon them are sent upon him. The station of Janab Salman is therefore very lofty. He is the only person in the entire dawat, throughout the entire Dawr al-Sitr, who became the Bab al-Abwab (Gate of Gates) for both the Nabi and the Wasi. He became the Bab al-Abwab for the Prophet, the Master of the Universe. Janab Khadijah had also become a Bab al-Abwab; Salman al-Farsi (ع) held that rank as well, and he likewise became the Bab al-Abwab of Janab Ali (ع).

"fa-qala lahu al-sail, ya Mawlai, kuntum bi-ashkhasiukum am bi-ayanikum. fa-qala lahu bal bi-ashkhasiina wa ayanina."

"So the questioner said to him: O my Master, were you there in your persons or in your representatives? And he said to him: Rather, in our persons and our representatives."

That is: were they present with their real selves or with their hijabs (veils)? The answer: with the real selves and with the hijabs both.

"wa amma al-Hajar al-Aswad wal-Rukn al-Asad fa-qad yakun wallahu alam anna qawl Sayyidna Sarim al-Din innahu ittasala bihi shayun latif mimma dakhkhiratuhu al-inayat al-ilahiyyah min hujub Amir al-Muminin al-mukanna 'anhu bil-ayn al-azimah al-nuraniyyah."

"As for the Black Stone and the Most Fortunate Corner, it may be, and Allah knows best, that the statement of Sayyidna Sarim al-Din is that a subtle substance was connected with it from what the divine providence stored from the veils of the Commander of the Faithful, who is alluded to as the Great, Luminous 'Ayn."

A subtle substance, drawn from what was stored by divine providence — namely the jussah-e-ibtidaiyyah of 'Ashir, taken from the hijabs of Amir al-Muminin, who is called the Ayn al-Azimah, the luminous one — was connected to his real self.

"wa amma qawluka wa hal yaqiu 'alayhi al-subhaniyyah, faqad sabbahatuhu al-malaikah al-qudsaniyyah haythu tashawwaqat ila tasawwur shakhsihi al-gharr, fa-awjada Allah taala subhanahu fil-samawati mithaluhu, fa-kanat tasbihuhu wa taqdisuhu laylan wa naharan ashiyyatan wa abkara, fa-kana hadha mithal azim."

"As for your statement, does the term Subhaniyyah apply to him: the holy angels have glorified him, when they yearned for the perception of his brilliant person. So Allah the Exalted, glory be to Him, brought into existence his likeness in the heavens, and they glorified and sanctified him night and day, evening and morning. And this was a great example."

The angels yearned to perceive his brilliant person — to behold him. In the spiritual realm they sought from Allah the didar (vision) of Amir al-Muminin. Though he is corporeally present on earth, they longed to behold him in the spiritual world and in the heavens. So Allah created a likeness of him in the heavens, and the angels glorified and sanctified him morning and evening, night and day.

"fa-kayfa bi-khalifat al-Ashir al-Hakim."

"So how is it with the Caliph of the 'Ashir, the Wise?"

As the Quranic verse says:

"fil-samai ilahun wa fil-ardi ilah."

"In the heaven is a god, and on the earth is a god."

This points to the state of Amir al-Muminin: in heaven there is an Ali and his likeness, and on earth there is an Ali whose likeness is in heaven.

"fa-kayfa bi-khalifat al-Ashir al-Hakim wa ma-ndimamuhu fi dimn al-Qaim al-hashir al-nashir."

"So how is it with the Caliph of the 'Ashir, the Wise, and his inclusion within the Qaim, the Gatherer, the Resurrector?"

His inclusion took place with the Qaim; he became the Bab al-Abwab for the Qaim. The Aimmah who came before — from Janab Hunayn to Amir al-Muminin — and the thalathah sufarah (the three emissaries), namely Mawlana 'Abd al-Muttalib, Mawlana Abdullah, and Mawlana Abu Talib, did not have their inclusion through Amir al-Muminin. Rather, they remained in the barzakh (intermediate state) of the Janab-e-Qaim, and the Qaim absorbed them directly, not through Amir al-Muminin. They hold a very high status. Up to Janab Hashim, Amir al-Muminin gathered the hayakil (هَيَاكِل) (structures) of the sufarah-e-nayyirah (luminous emissaries). After that, he gathered the hayakil from Janab Hasan to Abul-Qaim, who became the Bab al-Abwab of Qaim. It has never happened that an Imam gathered the Aimmah who came after him; yet this is among the extraordinary miracles of Amir al-Muminin — that he gathered the hayakil of the Imams who came later as well. His nafs-e-hissiyah (sensory soul) was so powerful and spiritual that it surpassed the hayakil of others, for only one whose nafs-e-hissiyah surpasses another's haykal (هَيْكَلٌ) can gather it.

His hashr (gathering) was therefore with the Qaim. He will become the caliph of the 'Ashir, the Mudabbir. By Ashir here is meant not that Ashir, but the jussah (جسّة) of this kawr; yawman ma (one day), through a progression in the line that has been formed, he will become the khalifah (caliph) within it — the Caliph of the Ashir. "wa suuduhu ila rutbat al-Ashir," and his ascent to the rank of the Ashir: his ascent will be as the Ashir, and he will be the jussah-e-ibtidaiyyah in which he will come, yawman ma.

"sabbahathu al-malaikah al-ruhaniyyah bi-ala min dhalika al-shan... li-man fatana al-maani al-rabbaniyyah."

"The spiritual angels glorified him with a station higher than that, for one who comprehends the Lordly meanings."

They glorified him with a station higher than any he had held before — higher than what he had attained across the various recurring cycles. In the seventh dawr (period), in the seventh zuhur (ظُهُور) (manifestation), this manifestation of his was the seventh, higher than all previous manifestations. It was because it was his seventh manifestation that he performed those extraordinary miracles. The angels glorified him with a glorification surpassing all previous manifestations, for the one who reflects deeply upon the Lordly meanings.

"wa amma qawluka kam hatta tabaddala al-mashriq maghriban wal-shimal junuban, fa-yakunu dhalika 'inda tarakhi al-rubatat, wa takunu al-tabdilat wal-istihalat."

"As for your statement, how long until the east has changed into the west and the north into the south: that will be at the loosening of the ties, and the changes and transformations will occur."

The tarakhi al-rubatat is the end of the kawr. Very great changes will occur then, and major events will take place, such that things will be entirely transformed.

"wa amma 'iddat dhalika fa-qad dhakarahu Sayyidna Humam."

"As for the period of that, Sayyidna Humam has mentioned it."

The duration has been mentioned by Sayyidna Humam al-Din and Sayyidna Sulayman bin Hasan, and those matters are to be consulted with the permission of the Wali al-Amr.

"wa fi aqwal dhil-jaddayn ma yujli al-sada wal-rayn."

"And in the sayings of Dhul-Jaddayn is that which clears away the rust and the stain."

Dhul-Jaddayn is Sayyidna Husayn bin Ahmad, a figure of immense stature. He wrote the tafsir (exegesis) of the Quran in seventy days and nights, on the command of Sayyidna Ali Sahab, who gave that command because Sayyidna Husayn bin Ahmad was the son of his sister. He was thirty-three years old when the command was given. He also performed Hajj on behalf of Sayyidna Jafar. Sayyidna Jafar, despite his great status as the twenty-eighth Dai and the first among the shumukh duat (lofty duat), did not himself perform Hajj; he had once set out for it but had to turn back due to certain difficulties. Sayyidna Ali Sahab therefore commanded: "You perform the Hajj of Sayyidna Sahab as a qada (make-up) and complete it." He did so. And when Sayyidna Ali Sahab commanded, "Husayn, write the tafsir of the Quran," he wrote it in seventy days and nights, even while traveling throughout that period. When he had completed it, a very swift scribe from Yemen took eight months to copy it. It fills three large volumes.

This is a magnificent state that Sayyidna Husayn bin Ahmad achieved. Although he was not a munfarid (solitary) dai, he holds immense standing; the duat take tawassul (intercession) through him, and Sayyidna Ismail bin Hibatullah Sahab refers to him as "Sayyidna Usama" in several places within the Kawakeb al-Durriyah — that great and magnificent book. Help is therefore to be sought from the sayings of Dhul-Jaddayn, which remove the rust that has settled upon hearts.

edits.chapter_key: beneath the kabah: lowlands, waters, and the well of the jinn
edits.body_md:
The fourth question: *al-sual al-rabi 'an al-bataih allati tahta al-Kabah, kam hiya* — "The fourth question, concerning the lowlands that are beneath the Kabah: how many are they?" — asks how many *bataih* (بِطَاحٌ) (lowlands) lie beneath the Kabah and how many they number. It continues with *wa min ayna abwabuhum* — "And from where are their gates?" — asking where their doors are; then *wa ma tasir wa yasiru ilayha* — "And what travels and goes toward it?" — what things go up to them; then *wa ma yadharu minha* — "And what appears from it?" — what things manifest from these *bataih*; and finally *wa Bir Dhat al-Alam alladhi qala al-shakhs al-azim* — "And the Well of Dhat al-Alam about which the great person spoke."

Bir Dhat al-Alam figures in the Battle of Bani Mustaliq. When the Prophet, salawatullahi 'alayhi, was returning from that expedition with his army, they came to a place whose people said: "We have a well in which there are shayatin who trouble us greatly, and all the people here are in distress." The Prophet commanded his army: "Who among you will go and fight them?" Two young men stepped forward. He said: "I give the guarantee of jannah to them" — that is, whoever fights these devils is guaranteed paradise. The two young men fought and were martyred. The Prophet then said to Ali (ع): "Qum ya Ali" — "Stand, O Ali" — that he should stand and fight them. Ali fought at Bir Dhat al-Alam, and when he emerged, blood was flowing from his sword. Rasulullah asked: "O Ali, how did you fight them?" He replied: "I fought them with my sword, and I fought them by reciting and blowing the verses of the Quran upon them." The verses of the Quran were so potent that he vanquished them through recitation and breath. He mentioned a third method as well, saying: "This is how I fought."

Bir Dhat al-Alam is thus the name of a well at which Amir al-Muminin fought. In one book, a question was put to a dai: were all the jinn whom Amir al-Muminin fought at Bir Dhat al-Alam destroyed? The dai answered: "No, they remain, but the coming Qaim will bring them to an end." The matter resembles that of *'adhab* (عَذَاب) (punishment) and *thawab* (reward) — the punishing of the enemies of the din — which the Aimmah do not finally determine. They leave that judgment to the Qaim, who is the Hashir and Nashir (Gatherer and Resurrector). The decision of whom to send to jannah and whom to send to the fire rests in part with Amir al-Muminin, who is Qasim al-Nar wal-Jannah (Distributor of the Fire and the Garden), and ultimately with the Qaim, who will pass the final judgment. He will cast the *azdad* (أَضْدَاد) (opposites) into Sakhr, and whatever decision he makes, he will make.

From the *'ulum* (knowledge), it can be understood that when the Qaim makes his *zuhur* (appearance) — at the occasion of Hajj — he will say to the Muminin: "On the yawm al-nahr, the day of Id, you kill the azdad." The Muminin will kill them, and this will continue for three days. After one or two days, such a stench will spread through the valley of Mina that the Muminin will find it difficult to breathe. They will plead to the Qaim: "We cannot endure this state, and yet we must remain in the valley of Mina until the thirteenth." The Imam will then command the winds, and winds will blow; the *manafidh* (مَنَافِذ) (outlets) of Sakhr — of which there are four — will draw those things away toward Sakhr. Sayyidna Ali Sahab has listed the names of those four *manafidh* in one of his books.

Asked where this well lies, he said: "I have not been able to determine where it is."

Among the miracles of Amir al-Muminin, from the perspective of the Qaim-e-Juzwi (partial Qaim), Bir Dhat al-Alam is likely counted as well.

The question continues: *Inni dhahabtu ila tahti mizab al-Kabah fi qissat qital al-jinn* — "I went under the water-spout of the Kabah in the story of the battle with the jinn." Amir al-Muminin said that he went under the *mizab* (water-spout) of the Kabah. Then *wal-mawaqif al-arba* — "and the four stations": the *mawaqif* (مَوَاقِفُ) are four. Then *wa min ayna manafidh al-bataih* — "And from where are the outlets of the lowlands?" — from where are the *manafidh* of the *bataih*, the windows. And finally *wa mannu bil-jawab fa-antum ahl al-sawab* — "So grant the favor of an answer, for you are the people of correctness": do the favor of giving the answer, for you are the people of correctness.

The reply opens: *al-jawab 'ala dhalika al-sual, naqulu bi-awn Allah al-Kabir al-Mutaal* — "The answer to that question: we say with the help of Allah, the Great, the Most High." The answer is offered with the help of Allah, the Great, the Most High, and with the grace of the Wali al-Asr wal-Zaman, alayhi salawat al-Rahim al-Rahman. And *wa tayid (تَأْيِيد) Mawlai al-Alam wa sirrihi al-ba' wal-muazzam* — "And with the support of my Master, the Most Learned, and his brilliant and magnificent secret" — that is, with the support of Sayyidna Hibatullah and his magnificent and luminous secret.

*anna al-bataih allati hawla al-qalb al-gharr hiya arba* — "that the lowlands which are around the brilliant heart are four." The *bataih* surrounding the luminous *qalb* (heart) are four, *kama sabaqa min al-qawl* — "as has been mentioned in the previous statement" — *li-man haqqaqa al-nazar* — "for one who has verified the observation." *wa qawluka innaha tahta al-bayt al-munir fa-laysa dhalika kadhalik bal hawlahu* — "And your statement that it is beneath the luminous House: it is not so; rather it is around it." The *bataih* do not lie beneath the Bayt al-Munir (Luminous House); they lie around it, on its peripheries, *'ala amrin jalilin khatir* — "upon a great and momentous affair." The *bataih* are on its peripheries, not beneath it.

*wa amma qawluka min ayna abwabuhum wa majariha* — "As for your statement, 'From where are their gates and their channels?'" — asking where their doors are and from where their channels flow. *wa amma ma yasadu minha wa yasiru ilayha* — "As for what ascends from it and what goes toward it" — things ascend and descend toward it. *fa-alam anna tahta al-qalb maun latif* — "So know that beneath the heart is a subtle water" — beneath the *qalb* there is a subtle water. *wa fi wasatihi* — "and in its center" — in its center too there is subtle water. *wa minhu yanbau ila tahti tilka al-bataih* — "And from it gushes forth to beneath those lowlands" — from those waters things ascend toward the *bataih*, *bi-majari* — "through channels" — channels that open, *wa manafidh* — "and outlets" — windows also being there, *'ala amrin sharif* — "upon a noble affair."

*wa hawla hadhihi al-bataih ahwiyah* — "And around these lowlands are atmospheres" — around these four *bataih* there are atmospheres: *al-sharifah al-shaffafah al-munirah* — "the noble, transparent, luminous ones" — transparent and luminous. *wa kadhalika hawla hadhihi al-bataih maun latif* — "And likewise, around these lowlands is a subtle water" — around the *bataih* there is also a very subtle water. *wa la yazal yasadu minha bukhar sharif* — "And a noble vapor does not cease to ascend from it" — noble vapors continuously ascend from these *bataih*. *wa huwa al-mizaj* — "And it is the temperament" — this is the *mizaj* (مِزَاجٌ) (temperament), *alladhi dhakarahu Sayyidna Hamid al-Din, alladhi takawwanat minhu nufus (نُفُوس) al-nuqa wal-aimmah al-mayamin* — "which Sayyidna Hamid al-Din mentioned, from which were formed the souls of the pure ones and the blessed Imams." This *mizaj*, rising from the subtle water and becoming vapor, was mentioned by Sayyidna Hamid al-Din al-Kirmani: from these vapors the *nufus* (souls) of the *nuqa* (نُقَاء) (pure ones) and the Aimmah al-Mayamin are formed.

*wa amma qawluka Bir Dhat al-Alam* — "As for your statement, 'the Well of Dhat al-Alam'" — that is, the question concerning Bir Dhat al-Alam — *wa qatluhu Amir al-Muminin al-muazzam al-jinn* — "and the killing of the jinn by the magnificent Commander of the Faithful" — *alladhina zaharu lamma daahum sallallahu 'alayhi fa-wallaw wa ankaru* — "who appeared when he, (ع), called them, but they turned away and denied." When Amir al-Muminin extended *dawat* (invitation) to them, they denied it and turned their backs. *fa-dhalika huwa al-qawl al-wadih al-sarih* — "So that is the clear, explicit statement" — the matter is true, clear, and explicit: Amir al-Muminin gave *dawat* to these jinn, and they denied it. In Surah al-Jinn it is stated that the jinn accepted faith; those were other jinn, whose states are described in that Surah.

*wal-hadith al-marwi al-sahih* — "And the authentic, transmitted hadith." *wa qatala minhum man zahara fi suwar al-haywaniyyah* — "And he killed from among them those who appeared in animal forms" — those who appeared in corporeal forms, he killed. *wa akhmada man tajarrada minhum fi surat al-zulmaniyyah* — "And he extinguished those among them who were divested in the form of darkness" — those in the *zulmani* (dark) form rather than the *haywani* (حَيَوَانِيّ) (animal) form, being *mujarrad* (مُجَرَّد) (abstract) among them, he destroyed and rendered motionless, *bil-hujaj al-wadihah* — "with the clear proofs" — *wal-barahin al-laihah* — "and the evident demonstrations" — for against those dark forms too the *hujaj* (حُجَج) (proofs) were established. *wa aslama minhum kathir* — "And many among them submitted" — many among them accepted faith and became Muslim (مُسْلِم). *wa la yunabbiuka mithlu khabir* — "And none can inform you like one who is well-acquainted" — no one else conveys these matters as they truly are.

*wa amma al-mawaqit fa-fiha asrar batinah wa zawahir kaminah* — "As for the miqats, in them are hidden secrets and latent manifestations." The *miqat* (مِيقَات) — the appointed place for entering ihram — holds hidden secrets and latent manifestations.

The miqats are five. The most excellent is Dhu al-Hulayfah, which is also called Bir Ali and Masjid al-Shajarah. It is the highest miqat, and the Hajj that the Prophet ﷺ performed — the single Hajj of the tenth year of Hijri — was commenced from this miqat. Great events are connected with it. The Prophet had taken Sayyidah Aishah with him, and she had her period at that time. She lamented greatly, and the Prophet said: "When Allah has made you weak and has made you deficient, then you must bear it," admonishing her firmly. He then moved forward, and many incidents occurred with his companions at the miqat.

All *riyat* and *fudulat* pass through the miqat. If a person does not enter ihram at the miqat and proceeds beyond it, he must turn back, return to the miqat, and make the *'aqd-e-niyyat* (firm intention) there. Such is the importance of the miqat: neither Hajj nor Umrah can take place without it, for the miqat is the *bab* (بَابٌ) (gate) to both.

The sixth miqat is a temporary one — Tanim, which is in fact Masjid Ali. It has become very grand; in earlier times it was a very small masjid. It is temporary in the sense that if a person arrives on the eighth of Dhu al-Hijjah with no time to reach the distant miqats such as al-Sail, he may make his *niyyat* (intention) at Tanim and join the pilgrimage. If he has still less time, he should proceed directly to 'Arafat, for standing at Arafat is what completes the Hajj. If a person does not reach Arafat, his Hajj is incomplete and has not been performed.

'Arafat is attributed to the Prophet. Three stations are visited: Mina, the main station, which belongs to Amir al-Muminin; Arafat, which belongs to Mawlana Rasulullah; and Muzdalifah, which belongs to Sayyidah Bibi Fatimah al-Zahra.

*Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. Allahumma ashraf al-fatiha hadiyyatan wa wasilatan saniyyatan zakiyyatan mardiyyatan ila arwah al-khamsat al-ashbah al-athar wa ila ruh Sayyidina Ali bin Hibatullah qaddas Allahu ruhahu wa anwara darihahu wa daafa 'alayna min barakatihi wa lazzatihi wa tayidatihi wa taqabbal minna ya Allah al-ifadah wal-istifadah bi-ahsani ma yakun bi-haqqi Sayyidina Muhammadin wa alihi ajmain wa sallim. Al-Fatihah.*

edits.chapter_key: harun to musa: the successor who dies before the prophet
edits.body_md:
A questioner raised a matter concerning the saying of Mawlana Zayd, upon him be the blessings of Allah, in the supplication for Wednesday. The supplication reads: *wa bayanihi fi al-manzilah* (and his statement in the station), and speaks of those who were second, *wa irsalihi wa muqasimuhu fi kulli shan* (and his sending and his divider in every matter). The questioner asked what this means, since the phrase stands in a supplication and its explanation is sought.

The supplication continues: *wa hayat al-manqul fi hayatihi* (and the life of the one who is transferred in his lifetime) — that is, the passing of one who dies during the lifetime of another. *Manahu Harun* (its meaning is Harun). *Wa kana nuqlatuhu Harun qabla Musa* (and his transfer was Harun before Musa). The one "transferred" is Harun, for Harun passed away before Musa. And the Prophet (صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَآلِهِ وَسَلَّمَ) said:

> *'Aliyyun minni bi-manzilati Haruna min Musa*

Ali holds toward him the same station that Harun held toward Musa. *Fa-la shakka anna nur al-azim 'Aliyyun (عَلِيٌّ) intaqala fi hayati nabiyyihi al-karim* (so there is no doubt that the great light, Ali, passed in the life of his noble Prophet). It is therefore beyond doubt that the great light of Ali passed away during the life of the Prophet.

Sayyidna Ismail ibn Hibatullah also noted that the awsiya (legatees) pass during the lives of their anbiya (prophets). The pattern holds for the aimmah as well: the passing occurs within the life of the imam or prophet they serve. So the passing of Ali (ع) too occurred in the life of the Prophet. Outwardly it did not happen in this way, but in reality it did.

The questioner continues: *bi-tafaddul wa-tatawwul* (with favor and bounty) — asking for favor and kindness. *Fa-qad akthartu* (for I have asked much): he has been asking many questions. *Wa ana asaluka* (and I ask you), with the plea that the answer not be given in a single sentence, for otherwise doubt will remain in him. *Wa maqal al-summa* (and a deafening statement): a word given as a mere concise phrase will not satisfy him. *Wa man yaftair sail* (and who is it that asks but a beggar): the one who asks is a beggar. *Wa man saala dhalla* (and he who asks is humbled): the one who asks is humbled. *Wa anta al-mukhtar fi al-itai wa al-mana* (and you have the choice in giving and withholding): the choice to grant or to refuse belongs to the one being asked, who may answer or decline. *Wa bayyin li* (and clarify for me): explain the supplication of Mawlana Zayd — the supplication already mentioned, whose praise is confirmed by his actions, pertaining to the fourth circle of power. It has been written that aid was given in his actions within that fourth power. What, then, are these circles? *Hal hiya min al-uqul* (are they from the intellects?), and to what does this point? *Wa qawl al-natiq li-Kalilah, istaqbili* (and the saying of the Natiq to Kalilah: "Come forward"): the saying of the *Natiq* — that is, of Rasulullah — to Kalilah, meaning to the jackal: "Come to me." *Al-aql al-khamis, sahib al-nur al-azam al-anwar, mufid al-khayrat wa muti al-fadail* (the fifth intellect, the owner of the greatest and most luminous light, the bestower of good things and the giver of virtues) — the one who benefits with charities and gives graces and great boons. *Ila an qala... zaharat al-qudar al-Fatimiyyah* (until he said... the Fatimi (فَاطِمِيّ) powers appeared). *Wa minhu ashraqat badayi al-suwar al-musawwarah* (and from him the splendors of the pictured forms shone forth) — its new matters. *Wa qad kharajtu fi suali min mana fi mana* (and I have digressed in my question from one meaning to another). *Awjaba al-hal... kasrat al-sual* (the situation necessitated... the abundance of questioning): his state is such that he asks more and more. *Wa antum min ahl al-ijzal* (and you are among the people of generosity): among the people of great generosity. The writer is himself very accomplished.

*Al-jawab 'ala dhalika al-sual* (the answer to that question). Sayyidna Ali ibn Hibah says: here is the answer to the question that has been asked. *Wa naqulu bi-awnillahi al-kabir al-mutaal* (and we say with the help of Allah, the Great, the Exalted), *wa minnati wali al-asr wa al-zaman* (and with the grace of the Master of the Age and Time), *alayhi salawat al-rahim al-rahman* (upon him be the blessings of the Merciful, the Compassionate), *wa tayid mawlaya al-alam al-alam al-anwar al-sirr al-bahir* (and the support of my master, the most learned scholar, the most luminous, the manifest secret). With the support of Mawlana Hibatullah — most luminous, whose secret is a luminous secret — this answer is given. *Al-muwasil li-suwar* (the one who connects to the forms): such a secret as is obtained by the forms. *An qawli Mawlana Zayd... salamu alayhi, al-malik al-ashir* (regarding the saying of Mawlana Zayd, (ع), the tenth king). By *al-malik al-ashir* is meant the Sayyid Dai. *Fa-dhalika huwa al-sirr al-khafi* (for that is the hidden secret): the matter pertains to a great and hidden secret, *alladhi la yustar bil-aqlam* (which is not written with pens) — not committed to writing. That is the nature of the question. *Wa la yulqa illa min lisanin ila udhun* (and it is not imparted except from a tongue to an ear): it is transmitted only from tongue to ear, not set down in writing, *mimman ala lahum al-maqam* (from those whose station is high).

*Wa dhalika annahu ilahun al-mufaddal al-awwal al-sabiqah fi al-adwar* (and that is because he is the favored god, the preceding first one in the cycles). He is the most favored, the first, the preceding, who has appeared across the cycles of old. As the Prophet said, *ana ibn al-karrat* (I am the son of the recurring appearances): he kept appearing through those recurring appearances, and Ali was always with him, appearing alongside. *Istakhlafat al-mim wa muwazin laha fi khafi al-asrar* (the *mim* became the successor, and it is its equivalent in the hidden secrets). The *mim* assumed the successorship *fi khafi asrarihi* (in his hidden secrets). *Wa kadhalika al-ayn idh ma istakhlafat al-qubbat al-Muhammadiyyah* (and similarly the *'ayn* (عَيْن), when it became the successor of the Muhammadan dome). In the same way the *ayn*, the *azimah* (عَزِيمَة), became the successor of the Muhammadan dome. *Wa raqa ila ufuq al-ashir* (and he ascended to the tenth horizon): having assumed the successorship, he ascended to the horizon of the tenth. *Al-munfarid bil-ahadiyyah* (the one unique in his uniqueness): he became unique in his oneness, with none like him.

A clarification arises here: did the *'ayn* take the successorship of the *mim*? Yes, the *ayn* took the successorship of the *mim*. The word there does not refer to the physical entity. Sometimes it refers to the *hijab*, and sometimes when the *muhtajib* is spoken of, the *hijab* is meant. The *mim* took the successorship from the *ayn*.

For the *muhtajib* of Ali, whose name is *'ayn*, is superior (أَفْضَل) to the *muhtajib* of Muhammad the Arab (صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم). Yet among the veils (حِجَابَات), the veil (حِجَابٌ) of the Prophet is superior to the veil of Ali.

Mawlana says regarding the three generations (الْقُرُونُ الثَّلَاثَةُ) that exist: they are the Messenger of God and Mawlana Ali. He says that Ali gathered the aimmah — from Hunayd to Hakim, and from Hasan to the Qaim — gathering them all. This was a rare thing: before him, no Imam had gathered another Imam who would come after him. But this is the station of Ali, that he is the first and the last (الْأَوَّلُ وَالْآخِرُ). "I am the first, and I am the last." He gathered the first ones and also gathered those who would come after. The three envoys (ثَلَاثَةُ سُفَرَاء) he did not gather in this same manner. The Prophet gathered Ali, and Ali too was gathered; it is a matter between them. As for the successorship of the *'ayn-i azimah* (عَيْنِ عَظِيمَةٍ), the first to assume it was Mawlana Abd al-Muttalib, after him Abu Talib (ع), and with Abu Talib was Abdullah (ع), *indallah* (with God). After that, the third successorship was taken by Ali, or by the Messenger; the Messenger took it. These successorships continue in this way, like a conjunction (قِرَانٌ). Abdullah is said to be *indallah*: Abdullah's station is with Allah, meaning with Abu Talib.

*Wa ihtajab bi-hijabi mim al-Maryamah* (and he was veiled by the veil of the *mim* of Mary). He adopted absence (غَيْبَة) through the veil of *mim-i Maryamah* (مِيمِ مَرْيَمَة). That is, the apparent passing of the Messenger was not truly the passing of the Messenger; rather, it was the passing of Ali's veil that occurred. In the remaining life that followed, the veil of Ali was at work. After the apparent passing of the Messenger, the one who appeared as Prophet lived for a further thirty years, and there was a gap of thirty years between the Prophet (ص) and Ali. Those thirty years during which he remained alive belonged to the veil of the Prophet and not to the veil of Ali. This is a rare matter.

*Wa thabata al-mim bi-hijab al-ayn* (and the *mim* was established by the veil of the *'ayn*). The *mim* remained established through the veil of the *ayn*. This event occurred on the day of Ghadir.

Is there proof for this in the noble Quran? Yes. The noble Quran states that the wife of the Messenger of God cannot remarry; no one else may marry her, for she is *Umm al-Muminin* (Mother of the Believers). Yet the Prophet (ص) had given Ali the choice that after his passing, Ali might divorce 'Aishah if the situation were as it is. Can one say this is possible? The intellect cannot grasp such things — not while he is working as the soul of the Messenger (نَفْسُ الرَّسُولِ). For this reason, in the *Mubahalah* as well:

> *Taalaw abnaana wa abnaakum wa nisaana wa nisaakum wa anfusana wa anfusakum*

Come, let us call our sons and your sons, our women and your women, and ourselves and yourselves. For "our sons and your sons" the Messenger brought Hasan and Husayn. For "our women and your women" there were several wives, yet he brought not one of them; instead he brought Fatimah al-Zahra (ع) on his own accord. And for "ourselves and yourselves" — meaning "bring our own people," *anfus* signifying one's own self — he brought Ali. This made clear that Ali was the soul of the Messenger.

*Talbisan 'ala qasir al-suwar* (as a deception upon those of limited forms). This deception was created for those who were weak-minded — those of limited forms. *Wa-ghusnan ala fi midajihi qudur* (and a branch upon... in his disposition... powers). Those who had powerful dispositions did not understand what had occurred. These states could be understood only by the highest-ranking believers.

*Wa kama azhara Mawlana Jafar al-Sadiq al-ghaybah bi-hijab waladihi Ismail* (and just as Mawlana Jafar al-Sadiq manifested the absence through the veil of his son Ismail). This is a well-known matter. Ismail (ع) passed away, but in reality it was Mawlana Jafar al-Sadiq who passed away through his son Ismail. In the gathering where Ismail had passed away and his body lay there, Imam Jafar al-Sadiq (ع) said, "Who will become my ransom (فِدْيَة)?" All the *hudud* of the *dawah* present — very high-ranking *hudud* — came forward saying, "O Mawla, we will, we will." But Furat ibn Ahmad, a person of the *hudud* of the *dawah*, sat with his head bowed in humility, thinking: what is my station and greatness, that the Imam, addressing a gathering in which he too was present, should ask who would become his veil (حِجَابٌ)? This humility was not hidden from the Imam. So he said, *Qum ya Furat* (Arise, O Furat). At that moment he recited the verse of Surah al-Muddaththir:

> *Ya ayyuha al-muddaththir, qum fa-andhir. Wa rabbaka fa-kabbir. Wa thiyabaka fa-tahhir*

O you who are wrapped in garments, arise and warn. And glorify your Lord. And purify your garments.

As soon as this verse was recited, people began greeting him: "Ya Imam al-Zaman" — O Imam, upon you be peace. When the Imam recited a verse upon a *hudud* of the *dawah*, that person's external garb was transformed. What state, then, must have been created when Jibril (ع), on behalf of Allah, came and recited this very verse upon the Messenger. *Kulla yawmin huwa fi shan* (every day He is in a new matter). Every day brings a new station. The master also says in one place that he never spent a single day without an increase in his knowledge: the knowledge he had yesterday was increased today. This was the state of Rasulullah — a state of great magnificence.

Mawlana Jafar al-Sadiq said to Furat, at the end: "I am you, and you are me." Something similar occurred in another Imam's time. A Sindhi man had come for the *ziyarah* of the Imam and was sitting in his presence. The Imam asked the gathering who would become his ransom, and everyone presented themselves and stood. But the Sindhi sat quietly. The Imam addressed him: "Why did you not stand?" And then he said, *Anta ana wa ana anta* (you are me and I am you). At that moment the Sindhi brother became a veil.

In Sindh too, if the historical record is examined, many scholars have passed and remarkable things occurred. In the time of Sayyidna Daud ibn Ajabshah, a person came to Ahmedabad who was an Agha Khani in religion and a horse merchant by trade — a very wealthy man whose name was Lad bin Dhannu. The word *Dhannu* is commonly written in that region and means rich (غَنِيّ), *dhan-wala*, one with wealth. Lad bin Dhannu came to Ahmedabad in connection with his horse trade. He was, however, a man of knowledge. Sayyidna Daud ibn Ajabshah met him and was greatly impressed by his character and his learning. When the time for prayer came, Sayyidna Daud said, "You may pray your prayer separately, and we will pray ours separately." But Lad bin Dhannu said, "No, Mawlana, I will pray with you, in your congregation." He prayed in that congregation, and afterward he joined the Ahl al-Sharif. Not only did he join, but as he deepened his study he accomplished such a remarkable feat that it is said of him that he became the *dai* for the Jazira of Sindh. And it is also said of him that he was the جامع, the compiler and gatherer, of a great assembly of poets. These too are wondrous and remarkable states that have come to pass.
