edits.chapter_key: the fifth intellect and the verdict on the caliphs
edits.body_md:
Maulana Ismail was seen in the veil of his father, and it became a mutual exchange — *fi sirrin jalilin*, in a great secret. *Wa lam yaqif 'ala ahl al-haqaiq tilka al-asrar*: the people of realities were not unaware of those secrets. *Wa kullu shayin indahu... inda rabbika bi-miqdar* — everything with the Lord is in a decreed measure. This supplication, *wa qawluhu fi hadha al-dua' al-madhkur fi shan Musa al-mashkur*, belongs to the station of the thankful Musa — that is, the supplication of Maulana Zayd — and it acts *bi-quwwat al-dairah al-rabiah*, by the power of the fourth circle, *al-mutashashiah anwaruha al-satiah*, whose brilliant and radiant lights spread in every direction.

The honorable Musa was the fourth among the *nutuqa* (نُطَقَاء), and the fourth is granted a special power. Among both the Imams and the *nutuqa*, the one who stands second and the one who stands fourth are each granted a particular strength. Among the Imams, Imam Husayn ibn Ali was granted a power by which he waged the greatest *jihad*. The fourth Imam, the honorable Baqir (ع), was granted a power by which he caused all the sayings of the honorable Prophet to be made manifest, expounding their interpretations and inner meanings. "O Baqir, split open knowledge," he was told — "O Muhammad, split open knowledge." That command became the source of his title. He conveyed this charge to Jabir ibn 'Abdullah al-Ansari, for the Prophet had said to Jabir: "My son's son — when you meet him, convey my peace to him." To convey peace is to convey the *tayid* and *mawaddah* that one carries; the bearer is the medium for it, and delivers it to its destination. Those were the circumstances.

Sayyidna Jabir ibn 'Abdullah al-Ansari was an elder of the very highest rank. He became a companion of the honorable Prophet and held great love for the honorable Ali. His deepest bond, however, was with the honorable Imam Baqir, and he lived an extraordinarily long life. On one occasion the Prophet said to him, "Go to that place." Jabir submitted, "O Mawla, I do not know that place; how should I go?" The Prophet gestured, pointing his finger, and from that finger a light emerged. "Follow this light," he said. "Wherever it is visible to you, go that way." By the guidance of that light Jabir set out on a long journey. He reached his destination, accomplished what he had been sent to do, delivered the Rasul's message, and completed his task. Afterward a thought came to him: long before, when he had once lost his way while carrying valuable goods, he had buried those goods beneath a bush somewhere nearby. He went to see whether that place still existed and whether the goods remained. He found the spot, dug the ground, and found the goods untouched. He took them with him, returned home, and then came before the Prophet. The Prophet said, "I sent you for one task, and you have returned having done two." Such was the honorable Jabir ibn Abdullah al-Ansari. His grave is in Alexandria, and a visitation was made there as well. He passed away in the time of the honorable Maulana Baqir, having lived a very long life, and he is visited to this day.

His son, 'Abdullah ibn Jabir, is in Iraq, in the mausoleum of Maulana Salman Farsi. Two are buried there. Maulana Tahir is also there — Tahir, the son of Maulana Baqir and brother of Imam Jafar al-Sadiq — and he too rests in Salman Pak, alongside Maulana Hudhayfah al-Yamani (حُذَيْفَةُ الْيَمَانِيُّ).

Hudhayfah al-Yamani holds a station of great significance. He was a companion of the Master and was present when, after the eighteenth — the day of Ghadir — Rasulullah undertook the journey toward Madinah. The hypocrites, the *munafiqin*, were burning with rage over the appointment of the honorable Ali, and they resolved to eliminate the Master himself. They formed a group, made their plan, and drew their daggers in the dark of night as the party traveled through a valley. By the power of God, Allah commanded the lightning to flash — and it flashed so continuously and so brightly that the Master was able to see every one of their faces. Hudhayfah al-Yamani stood with the honorable Prophet at that moment. The Prophet saw all their faces and said, "O Hudhayfah, did you see what I saw?" Hudhayfah replied, "O Rasulullah, what you saw, I saw." The Prophet said, "Keep this a secret; do not reveal it." And so Hudhayfah revealed it to no one. Yet the honorable 'Umar ibn al-Khattab would constantly press him: "Was I among that group that intended to kill the Prophet?" Hudhayfah held his silence — until finally Umar himself declared, *Wallahi, ana fihim*: "By God, I was among them." The question stands plain: men of that kind, who conspired to kill the Prophet, were they fit to become caliph?

A treatise by Nasir al-Din al-Tusi (نَصِيرُ الدِّينِ الطُّوسِيّ) addresses this question directly. In it, he dismantles the caliphs — and then Muawiyah and Yazid after them — with such precision that the work stands as essential reading. It is short, fifteen to twenty pages, yet the titles he applies to Abu Bakr are enough to make one's hair stand on end. The same holds for 'Umar and for Uthman.

As for whether Abu Bakr is counted among the *dais*, it is said that he was in the *dawah*. The reality with Abu Bakr is that from ancient times, from the earlier *dawah*, he had been a participant in the *dawah* of Abu Talib. He continued in that *dawah* and harbored a wish that he himself might be the awaited Prophet. When the Prophet ﷺ received prophethood and proclaimed the call of Islam, Abu Bakr accepted him — yet hypocrisy remained in his heart, and its expressions surfaced many times. One such expression was that the Master did not invite Abu Bakr along on the migration from Makkah to Madinah; the Prophet had intended to make the journey alone. Abu Bakr came along under the pretext of buying camels. He had learned of the plan because the Master, though he kept the matter of the migration secret, needed a fast camel and asked Abu Bakr for one. Abu Bakr agreed — but charged Rasulullah ten times the going rate for the camel.

Various such incidents are recorded. On one occasion Rasulullah was standing in the market and had struck a deal with a camel seller who had come from another city. The Prophet paid the agreed price and reached for the reins, saying, "Hand it over." The man said, "I will not hand it over. This camel is mine." A strange situation had arisen: the man had received his money but would not release the camel. At this point, according to the narrations, Abu Bakr and 'Umar were passing by. They asked, "O Rasulullah, what is the matter?" The Prophet explained: "This man came to sell a camel. I liked it, I paid the price, and now he will not hand it over." Abu Bakr and Umar then asked the Rasul, "Are you quite sure you paid the price?" At that the Prophet fell silent. By coincidence the honorable Ali also passed by and asked what was happening. The Master explained the same thing to Ali. Without another word Ali seized the man by the collar and said, "Return this camel." Afterward the Master asked Ali, "Why did you not do as the two Shaykhs did, and treat me the way they treated me?" Ali replied, "O Rasulullah, we have believed in you without seeing. We have not seen paradise, we have not seen hell, we have not seen the angels, we have not seen the hereafter, yet we have believed in all of it solely upon your word. Would we then not believe you in so small a matter as this?"

Many such incidents are recorded. One is the incident of the cave. Much is made of the fact that the honorable Rasul was with Abu Bakr in the cave, that Abu Bakr cradled the Prophet on his lap, and all manner of claims are advanced that do not hold up. The verse in Surah al-Tawbah says *idh huma fi al-ghar* — that they both were in the cave. This Allah acknowledges. And then: *fa-anzalallahu sakinatahu 'alayh* — Allah sent down His tranquility upon him. Two people were present, and tranquility descended upon one. No Muslim would dare to say that the tranquility — that special form of divine assistance — descended upon Abu Bakr while the honorable Prophet was left restless and helpless. Tranquility, then, descended upon the Rasul.

An objection might be raised: the Rasul is the Rasul and Abu Bakr is Abu Bakr; they are different, and of course tranquility descended upon the Prophet. But elsewhere — in Surah al-Fath and in Surah al-Tawbah itself — Allah says in another verse: *anzalallahu sakinatahu 'alayhi wa ala al-muminin* — Allah sent down His tranquility upon him and upon the believers. Tranquility descends upon the believers as well. Had Abu Bakr been among the believers, tranquility would have descended upon him too. A *dai* by the name of Shahriyar demonstrated this conclusively: since tranquility descends upon the believers, as the other verse makes plain, and no tranquility descended upon Abu Bakr in the cave, he was not even within the circle of faith. How, then, could such a person become caliph?

Then, when Rasulullah passed away, a gathering was convened at Saqifah Bani Saidah (سَاعِدَة) while the body of the Rasul lay unburied and without shroud. As Shaykh Sadi writes in his couplet: the dogs of the world, in their greed for worldly power, left the Prophet without his due.

There is also this point: as long as Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr was still in his father's loins, certain things were as they were. Abu Bakr's other son, 'Abd al-Rahman, and Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr — according to the narrations, both were absent in those moments. The narration specifically concerns Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr.

There is also the matter of the gap between the event of Ghadir and the Prophet's passing — two, three, perhaps four months — during which period history records that the Prophet dispatched Usamah (أُسَامَة) ibn Zayd on a military expedition, and these very men were placed under his command. They objected to being sent under the leadership of one so young; some said Usamah was seventeen, though the correct figure is twenty-eight and a half years old, the son of Harithah. They did not go. And Rasulullah, in his illness, kept asking by name: "Has Abu Bakr gone? Has 'Uthman gone? Has Umar ibn al-Khattab gone?"

The oath of allegiance was taken at Saqifah Bani Saidah — a place where thieves and robbers, after looting goods, would gather to divide their spoils among themselves. At that place the matter of the caliphate was decided. While the discussion was still underway, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab came forward at once and gave his oath of allegiance, declaring, "Whoever does not give the oath, my sword is on his head." That is how the oath was taken. God forbid. Today that place has been turned into a public bathhouse.

If this was a democracy, then in all three successions the principle of democracy was destroyed — in one case through nomination, in another through a council of six. It was all done in enmity toward Ali. The *dais* of high rank were not unaware of these matters. The ones the Prophet spoke of were indeed aware of all the sciences — Abu Bakr especially. But the greed of the world and the lust for rank led them to do all of this.

What happened to Muhsin bin Ali deserves reflection. He was so learned, so well read, that words fail to describe it. In the time of Sayyidna Husayn ibn Hasan, Sayyid 'Abdullah ibn Muhammad had been appointed, and Muhsin bin Ali stood behind Sayyidna Husayn ibn Hasan in prayer. Sayyid Abdullah ibn Muhammad would stand in such a way as to draw Muhsin close — half the space for himself and half for Muhsin. Such was their closeness. Sayyid Abdullah ibn Muhammad held such great friendship with Muhsin bin Ali that he always seated him at his side.

On Fridays, Sayyid Muhammad al-Jamali would come — he came only on Fridays, praying in his own mosques the rest of the time. Being senior, he would sit to the left of Sayyid Husayn bin Ismail, behind the Imam.

That was the time of Sayyidna Husayn. On a later occasion Muhsin was sitting behind him, and after Muhsin was Sayyid 'Abdullah. Once, when the summers began, the prayer was held in the courtyard. Sayyid Husayn bin Ismail led the Maghrib prayer. Then, in the interval between the two evening prayers, he sat awhile, rose, went into the prayer niche, and the congregation followed. He called Sayyid Abdullah Muhammad and said something to him, to which Sayyid Abdullah replied, "You pray your prayer, I will pray mine." At that point Muhsin led the prayer.

Affairs deteriorated considerably after that. Yet such had been the friendship between Sayyid 'Abdullah Muhammad and Muhsin. When the clarification came — after Sayyid sahib had tested Sayyid Abdullah Muhammad and Sayyid Ahmad al-Jamali for many years and then forgiven him — he performed the *nas* (appointment) and forgave him. So when Sayyid Abdullah ibn Muhammad became a *dai*, Muhsin came to him on the third day. He did not offer the full *musafahah* (مُصَافَحَة) (handshake of recognition); he merely shook hands and said, "You and I were at the same station." Sayyid Abdullah ibn Muhammad replied, "Yes, it is correct that you and I were at the same station. But from my station I have built a building. And you — you have remained on that same station." He had stayed where he was, while from that same station the *dai* had raised a great edifice of faith.

Abu Bakr was not among the confidants of the era of 'Isa. They are other individuals, outside the list of the righteous. Among the six names there are also common names. The teachers of the Rasul — and among them the confidants of the era of Isa, the six confidants who existed between the Rasul and Isa — were those who gathered the precious treasures of the teachings of Isa. Their joining occurred with the Rasul. Although they were the confidants of the era of Isa, they are also among the chosen ones of the *dawr* and hold a great station.

*Fa-hwa yushiru 'ala anna kulla aqlin min al-uqul al-sab' al-izam yanzuru ila man qabalahu min al-rutab al-nutuqa al-saba fi al-sarb wa al-nizam* — this indicates that every intellect among the seven great intellects looks toward the one opposite it among the seven ranks of the *nutuqa*, in their series and order.

Of the seven intellects: setting aside the First Intellect and the tenth, eight remain between them. From that count, the first emanated one — the one who became unique — is further excluded. Between the first emanated one and the tenth, then, stand seven intellects. Each of those seven gives material support to the one opposite it among the *nutuqa*. The third intellect supports the first among the *nutuqa*, that is, Adam (ع). The fourth intellect, the eternal one, supports the honorable Nuh. And so it proceeds.

*Wa amma qawl al-natiq li-Kalilah, thumma istaqbili al-aql al-khamis, dhu al-fadl wa al-fadilah, sahib al-nur al-azam al-anwar, mufid al-khayrat wa muti al-fadail, ila an qala 'alayhissalam wa al-salam minhu zaharat al-qudar al-Fatimiyyah* — this is the saying of the Natiq to Kalilah: "Then come forward to the fifth intellect, the possessor of grace and virtue, the possessor of the greatest and most luminous light, the bestower of good things and the giver of virtues," until he said (ع): "from him the Fatimi powers appeared."

*Fa-l-aql al-khamis 'arrafna fi hadha al-wajh wa al-mana huwa al-Husayn ibn Ali Amir al-Muminin, al-khamis min al-Nabi* — the fifth intellect, understood in this aspect and meaning, is al-Husayn ibn Ali Amir al-Muminin, the fifth from the Prophet. Within the *Panjatan-i Pak* (the Holy Five) — the honorable Prophet, the honorable Ali, the honorable Fatimah al-Zahra, Hasan, and Husayn — Husayn was the fifth. The reference is to this.

*Wa al-qudar al-Fatimiyyah, hum al-aimmah min awladihi* — the Fatimi powers are the *aimmah* from his progeny, that is, from the progeny of the honorable Imam Husayn. They are called the Fatimi powers.

*Wa awlad Maulana Fatim al-huda* — the children of our master Fatim, who guides.

*Wa minhum ashraqat badayi al-suwar al-musawwarat* — from them, that is from the *aimmah*, new and wondrous forms shone forth, and their advent radiated light.

*Wa bihim taharrakat al-mutaharrikat* — by them the movers moved. These are all spiritual matters and joinings to which the passage makes reference.

This passage is found in *Kanz al-Ulum*, the book written by Sayyidna Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Fad. There is also *Kanz al-Walad*, a different work. *Kanz al-Walad* was written by Sayyidna Ibrahim ibn Husayn al-Hamidi, the second *dai* after the first *dai* Sayyidna Dhuayb, and he wrote it for his son Sayyidna Hatim — to instruct a son who reaches the station of a *dai* in the things he must know. *Kanz al-Ulum*, by contrast, was written by Sayyidna Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Fad, who explains therein that the *aimmah* who appeared in succession from the progeny of the honorable Husayn ibn Ali are in one sense also called *Aimmah Fatimiyyin*, because they stand in awe and reverence of the station of the honorable Bibi Fatimah al-Zahra.

It is also said that whenever the honorable Fatimah came to the honorable Rasulullah, he would often rise and seat her in his own place. The reason was the gathering she carried with her — a gathering of such station that when the Master of the Universe perceived it, he would rise out of joy and to honor that gathering. That gathering was the gathering of the *muhtajibin* (مُحْتَجِبِينَ) of the *awsiya*, a most magnificent gathering. The honorable Fatimah had assembled the *muhtajibin* of all the *awsiya*, which caused the station of the *hijab* to increase. The states that belonged to Fatimah bint Muhammad were the states of the *hijab*, and when the station of the *muhtajib* increases, the station of the *hijab* increases accordingly.

Wherever the footsteps of the Rasul fall, there the footsteps of Fatimah will fall. The *khilafah* was established. Among the *duat*, there stands a question of awe and reverence: who should be appointed to the station of the *'ayn* — Bibi Fatimah al-Zahra or Ibrahim Khalilullah? Among them, who is the successor in the *khilafah* of the *ayn* after the Rasul? This matter has not been clarified. One of the *dain* (دَيْنٌ), Sayyidna Abdullah al-Ali, wrote a book in which — as the brother Mukarram Saifullah sahib had transcribed — he clarified that the successions of all the Imams until the Day of Judgment have been set out: who will become the successor of the *ayn-i azimah* after whom. A most magnificent book, in which every single point has been made clear.

*Wa bihim tajalla al-ayn al-azimah, 'ilmuhu, ulumuhu, wa biyutuhu, wa maqamatuhu al-fahimah* — through them, through the Imams of purity, the Great *Ayn* manifested: His knowledge, His sciences, His houses, and His exalted stations. The honorable Ali became the *muhtajib* for all the Imams, and they, the Imams, are His *hijab*. Such is the state, and such is the station of the Master of the Universe.

This matter — the station of the Master of the Universe and the station of the Imams — has been clarified in Surah al-Fatihah as follows. Sayyidna Hasan Khan bin 'Abd al-Malik observes that Allah began His word, after Bismillah, with *Al-hamdu lillahi rabb il-alamin* — All praise is due to Allah, the Lord of the worlds. *Al-hamd* is the *marifah* (definite) form; its *nakirah* (indefinite) form is *hamd*. The word *hamd* is composed of the letters *ha*, *mim*, and *dal*, with numerical values of eight, forty, and four respectively, giving a total of fifty-two. Fifty-two signifies the three — Muhammad, Ali, and Fatimah — together with the forty-nine Imams who extend to Abu al-Aimmah. After Abu al-Aimmah, the era of manifestation (دَوْرِ كَشْف) begins: the Mahdi of the end of time will come, and the manifestation will occur. The honorable Muhammad (ع), the honorable Ali, and the honorable Fatimah al-Zahra — these three, together with the forty-nine Imams — make fifty-two. In reciting *Al-hamdu lillahi rabb il-alamin*, they are recognized and affirmed.

God Almighty said: *Wa-bud rabbaka hatta yatiyak al-yaqin* — "and worship your Lord until there comes to you the certainty." Where the word *yaqin* (يَقِين) (certainty) is used, it also carries a reference to Amir al-Muminin. In the literal sense, *yaqin* means death: worship Allah until death. But it also means until the meeting with Ali, for after passing away the meeting will be with Ali, and he will ask questions.

As it is in the Quran, in Surah al-Zumar, the thirty-ninth surah: when the group is taken toward the heavens, they will be stopped and questioned. The commentators, both Sunni and Shia, hold that this question is the question of the love and *walayah* (وَلَايَة) of Ali — a position established by proof. In one's life, did one hold the correct *walayah* for Ali or not? That is the question that will be asked.

The Master said: if a person spends his entire life in worship in the blessed gap between the Rukn al-Asad and Maqam Ibrahim, such that his very joints become loose from the exertion, yet has no love for Ali in his heart, then Allah will cast him into hellfire headlong. For the essence of the matter is this: once, Rasulullah asked his companions, "What is the essence of faith?" Someone said prayer. The Rasul said, "No, prayer is not the essence of faith." Another said fasting, another said Hajj, another said jihad. For each the Rasul said, "Not this." Then the Rasul declared, "It is *walayah* and love," meaning the *walayah* for Ali is the essence of faith.

Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. O Allah, convey the blessings of these holy offerings, a gift and a means, pure and pleasing, to the souls of the Holy Five, our masters Muhammad, Ali, Fatimah, Hasan, and Husayn. Accept from us this benefit and utilization. May Allah sanctify the soul of our master Ali ibn Hibatullah, and accept, O Allah, this benefit and utilization in the best way possible, by the right of our master Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, and bless and grant them peace. Al-Fatihah. Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. Al-hamdu lillahi rabb il-alamin. Ar-rahman ar-rahim. Maliki yawm id-din. Iyyaka nabudu wa iyyaka nastain. Ihdina al-sirat al-mustaqim. Sirat alladhina anamta 'alayhim ghayril maghdubi alayhim wa la al-dallin. On behalf of Sayyidna, our master, the absolute Dai, the treasurer of the house of truth, Sharafuddin and Zeeshanuddin, Ghulam Husayn, son of Sayyidna Mansur the sanctified one, and for Walidna Nasrullah ibn Abdullah Hibatullah ibn Mansur the sanctified one, may Allah exalt his station, protect him and guard him, surround him and conceal him, suffice him and heal him from the evil of jinn and men, and from the evil of diseases, aches, pains, and calamities. From the evil of the treacherous workings of time and days, from the evil of the movements of hours and moments, and the glances of eyes, and the stumblings of feet, and the machinations of schemers. May He make good his end in goodness and well-being, protect him in the rest of his life, prolong his pure life, and guard him in the fortress of his lofty station. May He make his days pleasant in a good life and in the attainment of ranks and stations. O you who have been guided, may Allah grant us and you to be in the fortress of his dawah, and may He grant us and you the blessings of his stations. By the right of Sayyidna and our master, the Imam, the manifest one with magnificent authority, upon whom and upon his pure forefathers be blessings and peace. Al-Fatihah. Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim. Al-hamdu lillahi rabb il-alamin. Ar-rahman ar-rahim. Maliki yawm id-din. Iyyaka nabudu wa iyyaka nastain. Ihdina al-sirat al-mustaqim. Sirat alladhina anamta alayhim ghayril maghdubi alayhim wa la al-dallin.

edits.body_md:
The ninth question, *al-sual al-tasi 'an ziyarat al-qubur*, concerns the visitation of graves — *kayfa dhalika*, how it works — and *wa ma yahdurul-qasidina lil-ajsman*, what attends those who visit the interred bodies. When visitors present themselves at a grave, *kayfa shuurul-maqsud* — how does the one intended sense it? Do the dead perceive that a visitor has come?

The question also concerns Sayyidna 'Abdullah ibn Thamir (عَبْدُ اللهِ بْنُ ثَامِرٍ), a very high-ranking elder and *mubashshir al-nabi* — one who gave glad tidings of the prophet. He lived before the Prophet ﷺ, his birth and death both preceding him, and he gave tidings of the coming of the Huzur. He died in Najran, at the site of *Ukhdud* (أُخْدُود), mentioned in Surah al-Buruj. His grave was seen in that era left in very poor condition — nothing more than a mound of earth, with no care given to it. Later, in pictures, it appeared beautifully restored. When journeys for *dawat*s were made in the time of Sayyidna Husayn bin Hasan and the road passed through *Ukhdud*, Sayyidna Husayn bin Hasan would always recite an *iradah* (إِرَادَة) — a devotional prayer — for him, and would recite a *dua*.

> *wa qad sara lahu hadhihil-muddah al-madidah*

A long period has passed for him, the questioner notes. The questioner adds that he has begun asking many questions and has exceeded his means, but his state is one of deep trouble, and so he continues. The one addressed is from *ahl al-fadl wal-nawal* — the people of favor and bounty, generous givers of gifts.

### The Answer

*Al-jawab 'ala dhalika's-sual* — the answer to that question.

> *naqulu bi-awnillahil-Kabiril-Mutaal*

We say with the help of Allah, the Great, the Most High.

> *Wa mannat Waliyyil-Asri waz-Zaman, 'alayhi salawatur-Rahimir-Rahman*

And by the grace of the Master of the Era and the Time, upon him be the blessings of the Merciful, the Compassionate.

> *Wa taidi Mawlayi al-Alam*

And by the aid of my Master, the distinguished one, Mawlana Sayyidna Hibatullah.

> *Wa sirruhul-bahir bi-nurin-nazm, anna ziyarat al-qubur sirrun mastur, wa huwal-muttasil bi-dhalikal-haddi 'alal-ghurur*

And his manifest secret with the light of the order: the visitation of graves is a concealed secret, connected to that rank over deception.

The concealed secret of grave visitation is this: the visitor receives emanations — *fudul* — from the rank of the one whose grave is visited, a high rank indeed.

> *Li-yashfaa lahu 'inda jamii's-suwar*

So that he may intercede for him at the gathering of the forms.

The one visited intercedes for the visitor in those gatherings of *suwar* where he is present. The higher the rank, the greater the spiritual powers. In life, the *hudud* of the Dawah were angels *bil-quwwah* — in potential. After death, they become angels *bil-fil* — in actuality. It has also been stated elsewhere that when a visitor comes, the one visited senses the visit. The luminous form — *surat nayyirah* (صُورَةٌ نَيِّرَة) — of the one visited is always turned toward his *fudala* (فُضَلَاءُ), his spiritual particle. A person, wherever he may be sitting, keeps his thoughts on his home and everything within it; the mind stays with what is most precious even across distance. In the same way, the one who has passed away keeps his luminous form oriented toward what is most precious to him: his *fudala*, which is advancing. Such a one desires that this *fudala* progress as swiftly as possible and ascend into the *aflak*. Through the luminous form — which resides within the *hiyakil* (هَيَاكِل), the spiritual structures, or accompanies the *hudud 'aliyah*, the higher ranks, on its way toward the *Bab al-Abwab*, the Gate of Gates — an *ishraq* (إِشْرَاقٌ), an illumination, continuously emanates. When a believer enters the circle of that *ishraq*, he too receives benefit, and the one visited intercedes for him.

As the Master of the Universe stated: when children visit the graves of their parents, the parents sense their arrival and are as joyful as they were when those children were small and would come and sit in their laps. That same joy is felt by the mother and father. This is the saying of the Rasul — that parents become extremely happy upon their children's visitation and feel great pleasure. And when the children pray for them, recite Yasin, or perform *nazr* (نَذْر) and *niyaz*, the parents perceive all of it. This connects to the verse in Surah Bani Israil:

> *Rabbirhamhuma kama rabbayani saghira*

My Lord, have mercy upon them as they brought me up when I was small.

People often mispronounce it as *rabbiyani*, but the correct form is *rabbayani*. The meaning is: O Allah, have mercy on them just as they showed mercy to me when I was small. This *dua* should be recited both during a parent's lifetime and after their death — mercy is not reserved for after death alone. While parents are still living, children should pray for them with this Quranic supplication: O Allah, have mercy on them as they had mercy on me in my childhood.

If the visitor is of a higher rank than the one visited, the matter is reversed. Aid and help then flow from the higher visitor down to the lower one, just as water always flows from a higher surface to a lower one.

For the grave of a great elder or a prophet, there are holy traces. The *fudala* itself is no longer there, but the traces — the *athar* (آثَارٌ) — remain, and a trace still signifies something.

Yes, traces remain. Even without *fudala*, the *athar* endure. It is on account of these *athar* that the blessings of the grave persist. A bottle of *'itr* — perfume — after the perfume has been emptied out still retains the fragrance. In the same way, even after the *fudala'* has progressed onward, its *athar* remain at the grave. Indeed, the very site of the grave will become the place of its future *futteh*.

Yes, yes.

### Intercession and the Means

> *Wa li-yashfaa lahu 'inda majamii's-suwar, wa li-yakshifa anhu ma arahu min fununil-masaib*

To that extent, the various calamities befalling the visitor are removed by the one visited. And seek the means of approach to Him.

Among the common people, *'awam al-nas*, the misguided generally interpret this to mean: reach Allah through the Quran. That is not its meaning. The *marifat* (مَعْرِفَة) — the gnosis — of the Worshipped, the *mabud*, is contained within the *marifat* of the *hudud*, the ranks of the Dawah.

And what he knew of all the consequences —

that is, whatever affliction is befalling the visitor from various circumstances.

Because he is overseeing his *fudala*.

> *Wa yahummu 'alayha*

And he cares for it. He is deeply solicitous toward his *fudala*.

> *Wa yudabbiruha*

And he manages it — directing how to advance the *fudala* as swiftly as possible.

### The Degrees of Illumination

The lowest *ishraq* occurring — beyond which higher *ishraq*s also operate — is the *ishraq* of a believer's own *surat sharif* upon his body. Although the *surat sharif* is not yet fully formed at this stage, remaining at the level of *nafs namiyah* (the vegetative soul), *nafs hissiyah* (the sensory soul), and *nafs natiqah* (the rational soul), the *nafs natiqah* is nonetheless a *surat sharif* *bil-quwwah* — in potential — and its *ishraq* is already operating upon the body. This is the lowest *ishraq*. Above it come the higher *ishraq*s of the Imam and others.

The believer has been placed within Surat al-Fatiha. Surat al-Fatiha has seven verses, but its words — *kalimat* — number twenty-five. Those twenty-five words correspond to the twenty-five prophets mentioned in the glorious Quran. Although there are 124,000 prophets, Allah Taala has mentioned only twenty-five in the Quran, and Surat al-Fatiha likewise contains exactly twenty-five words. These twenty-five words indicate:

- Twelve *hudud* of the *jazair* — the islands — that is, the *duat* of the *jazair*, who are twelve.
- Twelve *hudud* of the *hadarat* — the presences — that is, the *duat* of the *hadarat*, who are twelve.

Their leader, the head of these twenty-four, is the Imam of the Time — making twenty-five in all.

The twelve *hudud* of the *jazair* each carry out their *dawat* at their own places, in their own languages, individually. The *duat* of the *hadarat*, however, operate where the manifestation of the Imam of the Time is present, and so their *dawat* is collective, not individual. This distinction is reflected in the *tahajjud* (تَهَجُّد) prayer, where two-*rakat* sets are offered in six *salam*s, because the *duat* of the *jazair* are connected in pairs — each *dai* has a companion. The *duat* of the *hadarat*, by contrast, carry out the *dawat* collectively, and their example is reflected in *salat al-layl* (صَلَاة اللَّيْل), whose twelve *rakat*s are prayed consecutively, all at once. After the *salat al-layl* there is a *dua*.

There is, there is.

Yes, a very long *dua*.

Yes, the *dua* is very long.

After no other prayer is there such a *dua*.

*Salat al-layl* is the final prayer before *shafa* (شَفْعٌ), and it indicates the *duat* of the *hadarat*. They are of very high rank, for it is from these very *duat* — from their *fudala* and their *riyad* — that the *Bab al-Salsal* (بَابُ السَّلْسَال) and the *Bab al-Anbiya* (بَابُ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ) are formed. These are people of the highest rank.

### Conscience and Choice

Conscience — *zamir*. A man's conscience does not allow him to do wrong; he feels it speaking to him. That is the guidance of the *natiqah*. The *natiqah* always seeks to keep its *namiyah* and *hissiyah* with it, and strives toward that end. The stronger the *natiqah*, the more powerfully it exerts *ishraq* upon its *namiyah*, its *hissiyah*, and upon the body, seeking to elevate them. This is why some *hudud* of the Dawah have been such that not only the *namiyah*, *hissiyah*, and *natiqah* join together after death to form the *surat sharif*, but even their internal organs and lower bodily parts ascend with them — on account of their nobility and the life of piety and purity they lived.

Conscience, however, is universal: everyone has one. And everyone has taken an oath. Some are bound by it; some are not. A man may say consciously, to his own conscience: "No, I am going to do this wrong thing." He then performs the act — whether right or wrong — with full intention. It is not that merely belonging to the Ahl al-Silsilah guarantees one walks the straight path. Free will — *ikhtiyar* (اِخْتِيَار) — exists.

Free will exists, and it is a very great thing that nature has given to man alone. Angels have not been given free will, for angels cannot sin, as the Quranic verse states:

> *wala yasun*

And they do not disobey.

They do not sin. Jannah and Dozakh — paradise and hell — have been made for humans alone. Among Allah's creations there are many: the moon, the sun, the *aflak*, the earth, animals, minerals, and countless other things. But Jannah and Dozakh are for humans alone, because man is the only creature with the choice — *ikhtiyar* — to do good and to do evil. Goodness is clear to him and evil is clear to him; yet knowing goodness, he may incline toward evil, and knowing evil, he may incline toward goodness. He has complete freedom of choice. Because of this choice, if he does good he draws near to Jannah, and if he does evil he draws near to Dozakh. This condition applies to man alone, not to others.

For the one endowed with *natiqah*, with *juzur*.

Yes. Among all of Allah's creation, it is man alone for whom Jannah and Dozakh have been created. There is a *dua* whose author urges that one should ask for Jannah five times daily and five times seek refuge from Dozakh:

> *Allahumma inni asalukal-jannah*

O Allah, I ask You for paradise.

> *Asalullahal-jannah*

I ask Allah for paradise.

> *Wa audhu billahi min al-nar*

And I seek refuge in Allah from the Fire — asking Allah for protection from Dozakh. This is prescribed to be done five times.

A slightly different tone is used for the *dua* after the *adhan*. *Rabbana atina* is in its own place. Here the asking is directly for Allah to grant Jannah, and the tone is different. That *dua* is in its own place — it is, in fact, the *dua* of Amir al-Muminin, what is recited after the *adhan*. Five times: some recite it five times at different times. And this one — five times together: five times to ask, and five times to seek refuge.

The *dua* after the *adhan* is apt because the interval between the *adhan* and the *iqamah* (إِقَامَة) is one of the five times when *dua*s are accepted. During that interval, supplications are answered. The prayer is offered, as Amir al-Muminin prescribed:

> *Allahumma inni asalukal-jannah... wa an tuzawwajani min al-huril-in*

O Allah, I ask You for paradise, and that You unite me with the maidens of paradise.

The *hur 'in* are in truth the *hudud aliyah* (حُدُودٌ عَالِيَة). The prayer is that unification — union — may be granted with the *hudud aliyah*.

### The Twenty-Eight Stages

The *zubad* (زُبَد) are these. After the *fudala* has progressed, it must travel to Baytullah. The great grave — as distinct from the small grave — is Baytullah; the small grave is the one in which a person is placed after death. To journey to Baytullah, there are twenty-eight stages, *manazil* (مَنَازِل), to cross. From the place where a person died, the *fudala* moves gradually:

- First it comes to the spot in the masjid where he used to pray. One who prays habitually makes a particular place his own, and that place becomes the gathering-point for his *fudala*.
- From there it progresses to the *mihrab* — the prayer niche.
- From the *mihrab* it advances to the shrine of Sayyidna Sulayman bin Hasan.

The progression continues. From Sayyidna Sulayman bin Hasan's shrine it moves onward through various noble places — *amakin sharifah* — until it reaches the *mawaqit*, the appointed stations: the five stations from which pilgrims bind their intention for *umrah*. It is said that *fudalat* and *riyad* gather at those stations. Progressing further, from Anderganj Charkhan the *fudala* arrives at the precincts of Baytullah, reaching the various *rukn* (رُكْنٌ)s — the corners — and ultimately arriving at the *rukn al-aswad*, the Black Stone corner. This process is ongoing and unceasing. From there it ascends.

The state of ascension is called *zubad*. While it rises, it remains in the state of *fudala*. When the *fudala* arrives at the pillars of Baytullah, it is called *zakhair* — treasures. When it ascends to the *aflak*, the celestial spheres, it is called *zubad*. The *zubad* is a very exalted state of being.

The *zubad sharifah* thus meet both the visitor and the one whose grave is visited, and they aid them.

> *Wa aydan fa-inna kullu qabrin damma hadhihil-hudud*

Every grave that contains these *hudud* is connected to these *hudud muazzamah* (حُدُودٌ مُعَظَّمَة).

> *Fa-tahtahu sirrun 'azim min al-khamairil-kaminah*

Beneath it lies a great secret from the latent leavens.

> *Fi tilkal-biqail-mukarramah*

Those are honored spots — their noble places.

> *Fa-li-dhalika wajabat ziyaratuha*

Their visitation therefore becomes obligatory. The hidden leavens are present there; the *suwar* cast their *ishraq* upon the grave; things have progressed while *athar* remain. For all these reasons visitation becomes obligatory. These places are exceedingly pure, and they benefit the believer and the visitor alike.

### Amanullah Saheb

A story of this kind occurred in the time of Wali al-Muqaddas. A man named Amanullah Saheb, who served as a *Mulla Adib* in the village of Taliwala, contracted cancer in his final days. The cancer was in his jaw, and his condition was grave. Various doctors examined him, yet the cancer continued to worsen. He was a man of firm faith with deep trust in Huzur. Taliwala lies very close to Khankhah Sharif — the nearest village to it. At Khankhah Sharif are two of the elders: Sayyidi Yusuf bin Ali Khan and Sayyidi Sharif Muhammad Saheb Sindhi. Amanullah Saheb would go there and sit as if in *itikaf* — in seclusion. He would take soil from that grave and apply it to the afflicted place. This became his daily routine, maintained for months. When he later returned to the doctors, the cancer had vanished entirely, and he was completely well.

This too reflects a principle at work. The masters of the graves, who lived noble lives, were *bil-quwwah* — in potentiality — during their lives, and have now become *bil-fil*, in actuality. By virtue of becoming *bil-fil*, they have the capacity to benefit their followers and those who hold faith in them. Benefit is received in this way.

Amanullah Saheb was the father of Salim, who recently built the hospital.

> *Allati la hadatah*

Without limit.

Those noble *suwar* meet both the visitor and the one whose grave is visited. The *suwar* are ever oriented toward their *fudala*, and because of this the *ishraq* continues uninterrupted — the *ishraq* of the *surah* toward its *fudala*. The person who comes to visit, dwelling within that circle, also receives benefit.

As has been mentioned, the soil of Imam Husayn's grave is indeed regarded as *khak-e-shifa* — soil of healing. There is also a saying of the Master of the Universe:

When the chests become constricted, seek help from the people of the graves.

When the chests become constricted — when no way out can be found, when the distress is such that a person cannot see how to remove his trouble — help is to be sought from the people of the graves. The saying does not say to seek help from Allah directly. Allah is the one who ultimately helps. The text before them read: *wa lahu shanun 'adhim wa maqamun jasim* — he has a great station and a lofty rank. His station is very great and his rank very high. The ranks of the *duat* are *rutab al-aliyah* (رُتَبٌ الْعَالِيَةُ), high ranks, and those ranks, along with the other ranks besides them, differ among themselves *fi 'uluww al-darajat* — in the loftiness of degrees. Rank is not of one type, for the degrees themselves are lofty.

*Li-anna kull al-martabah fi dhatiha sab rutab* — because every rank in itself has seven ranks — *yu-khafi min al-asrar al-thaniyah*, hidden from the second secrets. Every rank divides into seven ranks according to the high secrets that belong to it. If there is a *dai*, that one *dai* is divided into seven ranks, and among them is one who stands in the highest of the seven. Sometimes a *dai* stands in that highest rank.

*Inda dhawi al-adhan al-saqiyah* — with those of piercing intellect. *Wa minhum man yakunu fi awsatihi* — and among them is one who is in its middle. Some *duat* stand in the middle of these ranks, *tilka al-rutab al-madhkurah* — those mentioned ranks, whose mention has been made. And among them is one who is in the lowest rank; some *duat* stand at its lowest.

Asked who decides which rank a man occupies, he answered that it is the Imam of the time who decides which *dai* is in which rank, and that the declaration comes later. Succeeding *duat* say that so-and-so was in such a rank, that his rank was this. The matter is recorded in the books, and some *duat* have also expressed their ranks, saying that this one was in such-and-such a rank and that one in such-and-such a rank.

Among the *duat*, there are also those who, on account of their past *sawabit* (ثَوَابِت) and their *hasanat* — the good deeds that were theirs — come *ila adna rutab al-hujjiyah*, to the lowest rank of the *rutbah* (رُتْبَةٌ) of *hujjiyah* (حُجِّيَّة). They leave the rank of *dai* and enter the lowest rank of *hujjat*. *Ma fawqaha min rutab al-aliyah* — what lies above it from the high ranks — they may ascend to a rank even higher than that, since the rank of *hujjat* likewise contains several ranks, and they enter into those as well.

A *hujjat* is of two types:

- The rank above the *duat*, which is the rank of *hujjat*.
- The son of the Imam, who is also called a *hujjat*.

Asked about the *dai*s of the present day, he answered that all the *duat* who came after Sayyidna Sulayman bin Hasan, until the *Qiyamah*, were established in the rank of *hujjat*. Their ranks were elevated and they were established in the rank of *hujjat*. This is their *shan*. These are the *qaimiyyat* (قَائِمِيَّة) — the *duat* of the era of the *qaim* — for there are three eras:

1. The *dawr al-nabawi*
2. The *dawr al-tayyibi*
3. The *dawr al-qaimi* (دَوْرُ الْقَائِم)

The *dawr al-nabawi* lasted until Mawlana Ali al-Tayyib. After Mawlana Ali al-Tayyib came the *dawr al-tayyibi*, which lasted until Sayyidna Sulayman bin Hasan, after whom the *dawr al-qaimi* began. When one thousand years were completed, the *dawr al-qaimi* began.

*Wa minhum man yakunu mustawdaan* — and among them is one who is a temporary trustee. Among those *duat* there is this further distinction: some hold the rank of *mustawda*. *Wa minhum man yakunu mustaqarran fi al-istida* — and some are *mustaqarr* (مُسْتَقَرٌّ), permanent, within the *istida* (اسْتِعْدَاد). The *istida* is the rank of *duat*, and it is a *mustawda* rank, while the rank of the *aimmah* is *mustaqarr*. So within the *istida*, some are *mustawdain* (مُسْتَوْدَعِين) and some *duat* become *mustaqarrin* (مُسْتَقِرِّين).

Asked to point to an instance, he said that Sayyidna Sulayman bin Hasan — despite his learning and despite the greatness he possessed, of which an example had just been set before them — was in the rank of *mustawdain*, while Sayyidna Jafar bin Sulayman was *mustaqarr*. Other *duat* came after him. Not all the *duat* have been mentioned, but some *duat* became *mustaqarr*, and among them the first was Sayyidna Jafar bin Sulayman — who held the rank of *mustaqarr*, meaning that within the *istidaiyyat* he became *mustaqarr*. All are *mustawdain*, but within the *istidaiyyat* he became *mustaqarr*. So the rank of Sayyidna Jafar rose higher still, and he reached the station of *hujjiyah*.

When it was compared to the station of the Nabi, he said that the station of the Nabi is something else entirely. When asked for the definition of *mustaqarr* — and whether it meant the succession of son after father — he answered that it is not like that. That belongs only to the Imams; the lineage of son from father is among the Imams. But *mustawda* and *mustaqarr* mean something different from that, and their full explanation has not come down: their rank moves from *istida* toward *istiqrar* (اِسْتِقْرَار), permanence, and it is possible that they become masters of special *majami* (مَجَامِع). Allah knows best. When it was put to him that from *mustawda* to *mustaqarr* is higher, and that this is what the passage yields, he agreed, and said it could be that they become masters of *majami*, special ones, and that special support is obtained by them from the Imam.

Just so did Sayyidna Jafar receive it. When Sayyidna Jafar traveled to Janad — a place in Yemen — and entered the *masjid* there, he was on a journey. With him were Sayyidna Ibrahim, his brother and the son of Sayyidna Muhammad bin Fawz; Sayyidna Husayn bin Ahmad, his sister's son; and a Sindhi brother traveling in their company. Right at the time of *Maghrib*, when its hour was very near, Sayyidna Jafar said, "Look, at this moment the *tajalli* (تَجَلِّي) of the Imam is upon me. And at this moment, whatever *dua* you make, it will be accepted." So Sayyidna Ibrahim bin Muhammad bin Fawz made this *dua*: that his son should be a Dai and that the lineage of *duat* should continue in his progeny until the *Qiyamah*. Sayyidna Husayn bin Ahmad asked that he obtain such knowledge as neither the first ones had received nor the last ones. He then wrote such magnificent books — *Badiat al-Bayan*, and the *Hashiyah* on the *Anwar*, and others — that the *duat* are astonished and perplexed by them. The *duat mustaqarrin* (دُعَاةٌ مُسْتَقَرِّينَ) are astonished and perplexed by them. When they mention his name they call him Sayyidna Husam, though he was not *mustaqarr* and remained *ghayr munfarid* (غَيْرُ مُنْفَرِد); yet they mention his name with great respect and call him Sayyidna Husam. The Sindhi brother who was there had very poor handwriting, so he asked that his handwriting become very good. As the capacity of each was, so were the supplications, and his handwriting also became very good.

This narration used to be read in the *hijrat*, in the time of Sayyidna Husayn bin Hasan. Between *Maghrib* and *'Isha* the book of *Sirah* of the *duat* was read, and incidents from the *sirah* of the *duat* would come up. One time this incident came up, and Sayyidna Husayn bin Hasan looked at Ghulam and said, "Ghulam, you people are always worried about your handwriting." At that time Syedi Abdullah had arrived from Hindustan — Hadrat Abdullah sahib had arrived. And Sayyidna sahib said, "Mawlana, he was not a Hindi, he was a Sindhi."

Asked whether the man spoken of was Syedna Husayn bin Ahmad Dhul-Jaddayn, he said yes, Dhul-Jaddayn. The one in Baroda, however, is not Dhul-Jaddayn himself but Ali bin Husayn bin Ahmad bin Husayn bin Dhul-Jaddayn. Sayyidna Husayn bin Ahmad, whose story is told alongside Sayyidna Jafar, is his grandfather, and the one in Baroda is his grandson. He was sent in the time of Sayyidna Hibatullah, Ali bin Husayn. It is therefore a misunderstanding to say that the son of Dhul-Jaddayn lies there; the one buried there is not his son but his grandson. He passed away at forty-five years of age, in Baroda, and he was a great scholar — a very great scholar.

It was said that this is why Sayyidna Sulayman sahib always referred to Sayyidna Jafar as "my mawla." He answered: *Al-Mawla*. "Mawla Jafar, Mawla Jafar." How great a station it must be, that the father — in the *abyat* that Sayyidna Sulayman bin Hasan wrote describing the *shan* of Sayyidna Jafar bin Sulayman — used the words "Mawla Jafar, Mawla Jafar." Then Sayyidna Jafar, *qaddas Allahu ruhahu*, after his father's passing, transcribed those verses. His handwriting was very strange and unusual, completely unique. He transcribed them, and he removed the word "Mawla." When Sayyidna Sulayman sahib passed away, Sayyidna Jafar was eleven years old. Had he been much older when he was called "Mawla," the matter would be understandable; but at such a young age it was said, "my Mawla Jafar."

As for Ali bin Husayn just mentioned, his *rawdah* is the one called the *rawdah* of Dhul-Jaddayn. In it Hadrat Shakir sahib Muqaddas is also buried, and 'Azizah Bu as well — on one side Hadrat Shakir sahib Muqaddas, and on the other side Azizah Bu. It was observed that the day before had been his day, and he confirmed it.

When Sayyidna Ali bin Husayn al-Makrami came to Hindustan, Hadrat Shakir sahib Muqaddas was still alive. In Baroda, Hadrat Shakir sahib made this request: "Mawlana, my age has advanced, and *kullu nafsin dhaiqat al-mawt* — every soul will taste death — so I want to select the place of my burial, where I will be buried." Syedi sahib looked at all four sides and then said, "No, your place should be here," meaning where he was standing. There are four corners; in one corner he is buried, and in one corner is 'Azizah Bu, who was already there. He said, "This is your place." Asked whether Hadrat Shakir sahib had chosen another spot, he said yes, Hadrat Shakir sahib had thought of being near Dhul-Jaddayn, and Syedi sahib said, "This is the place."

Concerning Sayyidna Sulayman sahib and Sayyidna Jafar, it was asked whether what happened at the birth was not an indication that a Dai greater than himself had been born — for at that time Sayyidna Sulayman sahib had not yet become the Dai. He said yes. It was then the era of Sayyidna Daud bin 'Ajab Shah, who passed away in 999 Hijri. The matter belongs to a time before that: when Khadijah bint Nuh was pregnant and Sayyidna Jafar bin Sulayman was still in the womb, Sayyidna Sulayman sahib said to Janab Khadijah bint Nuh, "Your son is very blessed." She said, "Mawla, who knows whether it will be a boy or a girl?" He said, "It will be a boy, and he will be the Dai of his time." And he said also, "You will serve his *dawah* greatly." The believer sees with the light of Allah. The second thing that happened was that of Khadijah bint Nuh he used the term *rijal al-dawah* (رِجَال الدَّعْوَة), saying that she wears an earthly dress but in reality she is from the *rijal al-dawah*, one of the *rijal al-dawah*.

Sayyidna Muhammad bin Fawz, *'ala al-usul*, mentioned to Sayyidna Jafar, after the *intiqal* had happened, "I think that for the prosperity and well-being of the *dawah*, I should marry the wife of Sayyidna Sulayman bin Hasan." Sayyidna Jafar related this to his mother, and she said, "I will ponder this matter." After some time she agreed. So blessed a wife was she that from Sayyidna Sulayman bin Hasan, Sayyidna Yusuf bin Sulayman was born; and from Sayyidna Jafar bin Sulayman came Sayyidna Abd al-Tayyib and Sayyidna Ali. All four became *duat*:

- Sayyidna Yusuf and Sayyidna Abd al-Tayyib were *duat ghayr munfarid* (دُعَاةٌ غَيْرُ مُنْفَرِدٍ).
- Sayyidna Jafar and Sayyidna Ali sahib were *munfarid duat*.

Sayyidna Abd al-Tayyib wrote many books; his handwriting was very fast and very clear, and he wrote several works.

When Mawlana Khadijah bint Nuh became his wife, Sayyidna Ibrahim sahib was born, along with other children. Sayyidna Ibrahim sahib was imprisoned in Yemen by the Zaidi king and remained there for fourteen years. Of those fourteen years, Sayyidna Husayn bin Hasan used to say: "Ghulam, the love of you Hindustanis for the *duat* is astonishing and strange. Our grandfather, when he was in prison, a Hindustani brother was there who would perform *Hajj* for him." In those days the performance of *Hajj* was a very difficult task, accomplished with great hardship. "For our grandfather, a Hindustani brother would perform *Hajj* every year." That is a great distinction indeed.

It was observed that the lineage of *duat* continued through Sayyidna Ibrahim and not through any of his brothers. He confirmed it: the line passed through none of his brothers. Sayyidna Ibrahim sahib had appointed his son Ismail, but Ismail passed away during his father's lifetime, and so the appointment was conferred on Sayyidna Muhammad bin Ismail, his grandson. The appointment rested upon his grandson.

*Kama kana sayakun* — as it was, so it will be. *Wa ma 'ulima sayulam* — what was known will be known; as it has been known, so it will certainly be known again. *Wa ma taht al-shams shayun bi-jadid* — there is nothing new under the sun.

The covenant then follows: a covenant of Allah, which is very firm. *Wa mithaquhu al-shadid* — and His covenant is strong, very strong. *Alayka ayyuha al-akh al-said* — upon you, O fortunate brother, in protecting the secrets of *al-Aliy al-Majid* (الْعَلِيُّ الْمَجِيدُ). This noble covenant requires that the secrets of *al-Aliy al-Majid* be protected.

*Wa man nadhara ila hadha al-kitab bi-ghayr idhn al-dai al-majid* — whoever looks into this book without the permission of the glorious Dai, *aw mimman lahu 'adw al-ilm* — or without the permission of one who holds the reins of knowledge, that is, the one in whose hand lies the rein of knowledge, who makes decisions in the *dawah* and possesses sound and penetrating insight, standing high in rank — *fa-qad baria min al-Mubdi' al-Muid* — then he is free of the Originator, the Restorer.

And the saying: *man adhaa sirrana adhaqahu Allah bard al-hadid* — whoever spreads our secret, Allah will make him taste the coldness of iron. Whoever broadcasts the secret will be made to taste the punishment of cold iron — a punishment that places him at the northern or the southern pole. The punishments are three:

- *'adhab al-adna* (عَذَابُ الْأَدْنَى)
- *adhab al-awsat* (أَذْهَاب الْأَوْسَاط)
- *adhab al-akbar* (عَذَابُ الْأَكْبَرِ)

Such a person falls into the *adhab al-awsat*. Asked whether this applies equally to one who reads without permission, he confirmed that it does.

With that the book is concluded, alhamdulillah. *Al-Aliy al-Wahhab* — the High, the Bestower — with His praise, *wa al-salat wa al-salam 'ala sayyidina Muhammad* — and blessings and peace upon our master Muhammad — *al-muntaqil min al-aslab al-tahirah ila al-arham al-mutahharah* — the one who transferred from pure loins to purified wombs. He kept transferring from the pure loins of his forefathers into the pure and holy wombs. None of his ancestors committed *shirk*; they were all pure and clean, for they were the *aimmah* of their time. How could they have committed *shirk*? All of them were righteous, the very essence of the universe, the *aimmah* of the time.

*Wa 'ala akhihi wa wasiyyihi* — and upon his brother and his legatee. Janab Ibrahim had two sons, Ismail and Ishaq. The line here descends from Janab Ismail, not from Janab Ishaq. From the progeny of Janab Ismail came the *aimmah*, *mustaqarr*, and from the progeny of Janab Ishaq came the *anbiya'*. The station of Janab Ismail is very high: he was present with Janab Ibrahim in the building of the Kabah, in the placing of the Hajar al-Aswad, and in raising the walls; and the genesis of Zamzam came through his feet. All of this stands to his glory. Yet his rank is less than his son's, and his son Qaydar's rank is less than his own, because Qaydar is the seventh Imam.

*Wa sallallahu 'alayhi wa ala akhihi wa wasiyyihi* — and may Allah send blessings upon him and upon his brother and his legatee — *al-muin al-aimmah al-ghurr* — the helper of the brilliant Imams — *bi-wasitat al-pak* — through the medium of the Pure one — *fi al-sirr al-mustasirr* — in the hidden secret. *Wa ala al-aimmah al-akhyar, majami' al-anwar* — and upon the righteous Imams, the collections of lights. *Wa 'ala Imam al-zaman, al-natiq, al-mubdi'... fi hal al-wiladah bi-alaniyah* — and upon the Imam of the time, the speaker, the originator, who at the moment of birth spoke openly. *Wa al-radi fi hadd al-tufuliyyah ila awan al-zuhur bi-nuraniyyah* — and the infant at the stage of childhood until the time of manifestation with luminosity. He progressed from childhood toward manifestation until his manifestation came with *nuraniyyah* (نُورَانِيَّةٌ). *Wa sallam 'alayhim* — and (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ).

Asked of whom this speaks, he answered that it speaks of the Imam of the time, whose rank is such that *Mubdi Taala* spoke with him openly in the state of *wiladah*, and who progressed from childhood toward manifestation until his manifestation came with *nuraniyyah*. And — and upon their forefathers, and upon their pure progeny, and upon their *duat*, who are *al-mayamin* — noble and honorable — *al-naibina manabahum ila qiyam yawm al-din* — their representatives until the establishment of the Day of Judgment.

It was then objected that the mention of *Mubdi Taala* here seems too elevated — that 'Aql al-Awwal or Aql al-Thani would make sense, but *Mubdi' Taala* would not, and that such a mention appears nowhere else. He answered that the term *Mubdi* (المُبدِع) may have been used while the reference is to the ranks below it. By *Mubdi Taala* the intent is not the one who brought existence from non-existence. That is not the intent — for what he did was to bring existence from non-existence, and that act was finished. After it, he has no further action. He has no further action at all. It was asked whether he would perform that act again, bringing existence once more from non-existence, and the answer was that he will never do so, that he will not do it again. It was asked: "What? Does he not have the power?" The answer came: "No — despite having the power, he will not do this." As for him — since when he is, what he is, what he is doing, and why he did it — the *duat* have no answer. There is only this: that he did it, and it was his *tafaddul* (تَفَضُّل) and his *mihrabani* that he did such a thing. That is the whole of the answer.

'Aql al-Awwal stands next. From the *marifah* he had of *Mubdi' Taala*, 'Aql al-Awwal became a *hijab* and a *bab*, and a continuous, flowing knowledge was established upon him that can never stop. For this reason it is said: *la takhudhuhu sinatun wa la nawm* — neither slumber nor sleep overtakes him. He feels no drowsiness and is not overcome by sleep, this Aql al-Awwal. Drowsiness makes a person partially heedless; sleep makes him completely heedless. Aql al-Awwal is neither partially heedless nor completely heedless. And *al-Hayy al-Qayyum* — the Living, the Self-Sustaining — he has become: alive and life-giving. *Al-Hayy al-Qayyum* is one of Allah's names and among the highest, and within it the *Ism al-Adham* is present. Certain words carry this quality — as is said of *Dhu al-Jalal wa al-Ikram* (ذُو الْجَلَالِ وَالْإِكْرَامِ) and *Ya Dha al-Jalal wa al-Ikram*, that within them the *Ism al-Adham* is present; so too *al-Hayy al-Qayyum*, which is the *tasbih* for Sunday. *Al-Hayy al-Qayyum* thus points toward Aql al-Awwal: that he is alive and life-giving.

What then did he do? The substance and support that 'Aql al-Awwal received from *Mubdi' Taala* he gave to 'Aql al-Thani — that is, to al-Munbaith al-Awwal — but only two and a half percent of it. He gave two and a half percent, as in *zakat*: of all that had gathered with him, he gave a portion of two and a half percent, because had he given the whole, his existence would have been consumed. In the same way, al-Munbaith al-Awwal gave to the ranks below him two and a half percent of his own. And so it continued.

> **Editorial note (tradition-grounded).** 
> A note on a word this chapter turns on: *hijrah* comes from the Arabic root ه-ج-ر, which carries
> the sense of breaking away and leaving a thing behind — cutting the ties that bind a person to a
> place. The wider tradition preserves this root in its most famous instance, the Prophet's
> emigration from Mecca to Medina, a departure so decisive that the Muslim calendar takes its
> beginning from it. Hearing that weight in the word helps a modern reader understand why a *Dar
> al-Hijrah* — a house built at the site of such a departure — is treated here as worth
> commemorating centuries later, and why the text can say that a man migrated from his land and
> his city "except on account of the greatness of his station": the leaving is not flight but a
> severance undertaken deliberately, and the place of it is remembered accordingly.

edits.chapter_key: the mahdi, the qaim, and the straight path
edits.body_md:
The first question concerns *Mawlana Mehdi* (مَوْلَانَا مَهْدِي), *sallallahu alayhi*. Two figures bear the name *Mehdi*: the eleventh Imam, who is *Mehdi*, and the fiftieth Imam, who is likewise a *Mehdi*.

The fiftieth is, in a certain sense, of the same order as *Rasulullah*: he does not fall within the circle of *Imamat* (إِمَامَة). *Mehdi Akhir al-Zaman* (مَهْدِيُّ آخِرِ الزَّمَان), the last *Mehdi*, stands outside that circle in the same way. He is neither an Imam nor the son of an Imam, yet his station (شَأْن) is immense. He is also called *Mim-e-Akhirah*. *Mim-e-Ula* is *Rasulullah*, *'ala dhikrihis salaam*, and *Mim-e-Akhirah* is *Mawlana Mehdi*, the fiftieth Imam.

The parallel has a precise significance. Just as *Rasulullah* broke the chain (سِلْك) of *Imamat* — being the twenty-ninth person to break that chain — so too did *Mawlana Mehdi* break it. After the forty-ninth Imam, the *Qaim* was due to come; but *Mawlana Mehdi* came in between. Today's Imam is *Abul Qaim* (أَبُو الْقَائِم), and after *Abul Qaim* the *Qaim* should have followed. *Mawlana Mehdi* came in between owing to his great precedents (سَوَابِقَات) and his exalted station.

The forefathers (جَدٌّ) of *Janab-e-Mehdi* were nonetheless Imams — just as the forefathers of *Rasulullah* were, though his immediate father was not.

A question was then raised, drawing upon a Quranic verse. God the Exalted said:

> *Taruj al-malaikatu wa al-ruh ilayhi fi yawmin kana miqdaruhu khamsina alfa sanah*

The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a day whose measure is fifty thousand years.

The question turned on *Fa mana al-yawm 'alayhi sallallahu alayhi wa al-dawr al-adhim, dawr al-kashf* (دَوْرُ الْكَشْف): the meaning of "the day" for him, (ع), is the great cycle, the cycle of unveiling (كَشْف). From *Janab-e-Mehdi* the cycle of *kashf* began; his cycle is called the cycle of *kashf*.

It is recalled that while studying with *Sayyidna Husayn bin Ismail*, the notion arose that *Mehdi* and *Qaim* are distinct. He said:

> *Al-Mehdi huwal Qaim, wal Qaim huwal Mehdi*

The Mehdi is the Qaim, and the Qaim is the Mehdi.

And he cautioned against treating them as two separate figures.

The question continued: *Fa al-mana 'alayhi sallallahu alayhi wa al-dawr al-adhim, dawr al-kashf, wa lahu mutimmoona min waladihi, wa huwa yakhudh zakaa* (زَكَاء). The meaning for him is the great cycle, the cycle of unveiling; for him are completers (مُتَمِّمِين) from his progeny; and he will receive the *khilafah* of *zakaa*, meaning the sun. The word *zakaa* appears in a *munajat* recited in *Sadaqallah*, composed by *Khassa Amir bin Sab*, where it is written: *Antum al-zakaa wa al-nasu*, "You are the sun, and the people are..." — meaning that *Janab-e-Ali* holds the position of the sun while others hold the position of stars.

As for the term *mutimmin*: just as there were *mutimmin* at the close of the cycle of 'Isa — those who come at the end of a *dawr*, or at the beginning of a *dawr*, being called *mutimmin* — so in the progeny of *Mawlana Mehdi* there is a *mutim*.

*Wa kam takunu khidmatuhu? Wa yakhudh khilafat al-ashir*: And what will his service be? He will receive the *khilafah* of the *'Ashir*. *Tafaddal alayna ya mawda' al-sirri wa al-sarair*: Bestow upon us, O repository of secrets and hidden matters. *Jazakallahu afdal al-jaza*: May Allah reward you with the best of rewards. *Bi-haqqi Sayyidina Muhammadin wa aalihi al-tahirin*: By the right of our master Muhammad and his pure family.

The answer follows. *Bi-awnillahi subhanahu wa mannihi wa yusrihi wa tayidi mawlana al-Malik, mahbat ashat al-malaik*: with the help of Allah, Glorified is He, and His grace and His ease, and the support of our master the King, namely *Sayyidna Hibatullah*, the place where the rays of the angels descend. *Anna mawlana al-Mehdi al-adhim, alladhi huwa qaim dawr al-sitr*: our master, the great *Mehdi*, is in truth the *Qaim* of the cycle of concealment (دَوْرُ السِّتْر).

*Wa lahu shanun 'adhim*, his station is very great; *wa fadlun jasim*, his virtue is immense. The author describes him not as a confluence (*jami'*) but as the *Qaim* of the *dawr al-sitr*. *Wa huwa majma thaman suwar, suwar 'idham samiyah*: he is the confluence of eight surahs, surahs of great and lofty rank. This rests upon the verse:

> *Wa yahmilu 'arsha rabbika fawqahum yawmaidhin thamaniyah*

And on that Day, eight will carry the Throne of your Lord above them.

That is, eight angels will bear the Divine Throne on the Day of Resurrection. *Wa sabu suwarin fi dawr al-kashf al-madi li-hadha al-shakhs*: and seven surahs belong to the past cycle of unveiling for this person, a *surah* having come every seven thousand years in the past *dawr al-kashf*. On this matter *Sayyidna 'Ali bin Hanzala* (سَيِّدُنَا عَلِيُّ بْنُ حَنْظَلَةَ), may Allah sanctify his soul, is cited: *Wa hiya yasadu fi asnaihi min suwar, sabun min al-qism alladhi, azimah fi thalathat alaf fi dawr al-fatrah* — and it ascends in its midst from the surahs, seven from the portion which is great, in three thousand years in the period of interruption (دَوْرُ الْفَتْرَة). These are three surahs, each representing one thousand years, yielding three in all.

*Wa hadha dawr al-sitr al-mutaqallibina fihi ahl al-sharra*: this is the cycle of concealment, in which evil people have prevailed. *Wa yawmuhu huwa dawr al-asna*: his day is the lofty cycle. *Wa al-imamah fihi mustamirrah*: the *Imamat* within it is continuous, as it was throughout the *dawr al-sitr*. *Min dhurriyyatihi, alladhina hum maani al-asma al-husna*: from his progeny, who are the meanings of the Most Beautiful Names.

*Wa dhakarta annahu yakhudh zakaa, fa-laysa dhalika kadhalik. Bal alladhi yakhudhuha bada intiha al-rubatati huwa al-rukn al-asham*: the questioner mentioned that he will receive the *khilafah* of the sun, but that is not so. Rather, the one who will receive it after the end of the four (رُبَاطَاتٌ) is the lofty pillar (الرُّكْنُ الْأَشَمُّ), meaning the *rukn al-asad* (رُكْنُ الْأَسَدِ), who will receive the *khilafah* of the sun.

*Fa-rif dhalika wa taaqqal ma hunalika. Wa 'alayka bi-al-tasawwur al-mustaqim. Li-takuna min sukkan jannat al-naim*: so understand this matter and comprehend what is there, and hold fast to straight understanding, so as to be among the dwellers of the Garden of Bliss.

*Wa amma al-Qaim, 'alayhi salamu, wa tahiyyatuhu wa ikramuhu, fa-innahu inda firaqi min hadhihi al-dar, yakhluf al-ashir*: as for the *Qaim*, may peace and greetings and honor be upon him, upon departure from this abode — at the time of passing away — he will succeed the *Ashir*.

A question arises concerning how long the *Qaim* will remain in the world. Only three days. The *qiyam* of the *Qaim* will last three days.

Whether the *Qaim* and *Mehdi Akhir al-Zaman* are two distinct personalities: they are indeed two distinct personalities. The *Qaim* of the *dawr al-sitr*, however, has been called *Mehdi*, and the station of *Mawlana Qaim* (مَوْلَانَا الْقَائِم) is certainly greater than that of *Mehdi*. That *Qaim*, peace be upon his mention, will receive the *khilafah* of the *'Ashir Aziz al-Jabbar*. The *Ashir* here refers to the second *juzi dai* (جُزْئِيّ دَاعِي) of this *kawr*. When he progresses beyond one *kawr*, he will become the *juzi dai* of the next *kawr*, and that will be the *Qaim* — and that too in a *juzi* (جُزْئِيٌّ) capacity, a partial one, not in a *kulli*, total, capacity, for many others stand in the line ahead.

The opening of Surah Ya-Sin illumines this:

> *Yasin. Wal-Quran al-hakim, innaka la-mina al-mursalin, 'ala siratin mustaqim*

Ya-Sin. By the wise Quran, indeed you are from among the messengers, on a straight path.

Allah grants such greatness as to say that he is from among the messengers, and then adds that he is on the straight path. At first this seems incongruous — like introducing a man as a PhD professor holding degrees from ten universities and then adding that he has passed his matriculation examination. Yet the meaning becomes clear: *'ala siratin mustaqim* refers to that line, the line of *juz's* (جُزْء), and among those standing in it the Prophet, (ع), is one. Before him in that line stand the *Thalathat Kubara'*, the Three Great Ones, and after them it is he.

There is a further verse in which Allah says:

> *Inna rabbi 'ala siratin mustaqim*

Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path.

This is also reported as a saying of the Prophet, that his Lord is on the straight path — referring to Abu Talib, the one who raised him, affirming that he too is on that path. From all of this, *sirat mustaqim* (صِرَاط مُسْتَقِيم) signifies this very path of *juz's*; it is the straight path. Yet for the *Aimmah al-Tahirin*, the Pure Imams, and for *Rasulullah*, the *sirat mustaqim* carries a different and higher meaning.

The recitation of *Ihdina al-sirat al-mustaqim*, "Guide us to the straight path," is a magnificent prayer. As *Haddrat al-Muqaddas* (حَضْرَةُ الْمُقَدَّس) once explained, it does not merely mean "place us on the straight path" but rather "make us walk upon it" — cause us to move forward along it. The chain extending from a *mumin* to the Imam passes through both the lower ranks (حُدُودٌ دَانِيَة) and the higher ranks (*hudud 'aliyah*). To walk that path is to move swiftly toward the *Bab al-Abwab*, which is the destination of every *mumin*s spiritual form (صُورَة). When that station of *Bab al-Abwab* is reached and its magnificent assembly — *fasl al-khitab*, the decisive speech — is attained, and when the Imam receives that assembly and conveys it to the *Farzand-e-Imam*, the son of the Imam, it becomes as it were a fixed deposit: wherever the *Farzand-e-Imam* goes, it accompanies them.

There are therefore two kinds of spiritual progress (تَرَقِّيَات):

- One in which a person strives and advances through their own effort.
- Another in which one advances by sitting in the lap of another, resting in that nearness.

Both are genuine forms of progress. The pace of advancement depends on each person's capacity, their *taqwa*, piety, and their *taharat* (طَهَارَة), purity. Furthermore, the *sadaqat*, charities, and good deeds performed after a *mumin*'s passing — when children recite on his behalf and perform righteous acts — reach him as well, causing him to progress more swiftly from whatever station he has attained.

A human's *surah* is not divided among the Imams; all the units gather in one place. A *surah sharif* that is progressing keeps on progressing. Whatever comes into the world — as a person passes away and after a thousand years returns — comes back in the same way, but minus the vegetative soul (نَامِيَة), minus the sensory soul (حِسِّيَّة), minus the rational soul (نَاطِقَة). Sometimes it even rises above his *moththalan ikhtirai*, his archetypal form. Its progress is very slow, yet it keeps progressing. In one *kawr*, its manifestations (ظُهُورَات) occur three hundred and sixty times, through the integration of the *walad*. For this reason *Sayyidna Ali bin Sulayman* said that in the human body there are three hundred and sixty *nufus*. This means that one of his *nafs* progresses in one *kawr*, in one *dawr*. When his integration through grace takes place, then one part out of three hundred and sixty progresses.

In the *duas* of *Mawlana Jafar al-Sadiq*, which are to be recited daily, there occurs in the twenty-seventh *tariqah* (طَرِيقَة) the phrase *Innaka 'ala siratin mustaqim*, "Indeed, you are on a straight path." Its address appears to be to Allah, as though saying, "O Allah, you are on the straight path." The answer is the same as before. "Allah" there does not mean *Mubdi' Taala*, the Originator, the Exalted, but the *juzi dai*, the partial missionary, of that *kawr*. The indication is toward him — that he too is on the *sirat mustaqim*, meaning that he stands in the line to take the *khilafah* of the *'Ashir*.

Everyone has to progress. *Allati ma yuhitu biha illa man safat suratuhu min al-rayb*: which cannot be encompassed except by one whose form has been purified from doubt. These matters can be understood and encompassed only by one whose *surah* has been completely purified from doubts and suspicions. *Wa tawalla amra 'alam al-tabiah*: and he took charge of the affair of the world of nature. Such ones become masters of the affairs of the natural world. *Wa yadharu fi afwaniha surur al-badiah… Fa-hafiz hadha al-jawab al-mukhtasar wa sunhu fa-innahu min al-sirr al-akbar*: and in its horizons appear wondrous joys; so preserve this concise answer and guard it, for it is from the greatest of secrets. This concise answer is to be known and guarded, for it is among the loftiest of secrets.

Here the matter rests for today, the need having been met.
